speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON GENEVA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I returned last night from attending the conference on the situation in Laos which, as hon. members know, has been going on in Geneva for about five weeks. I went back to Geneva to attend this conference having in mind four objectives. The first was to do whatever was possible to get the conference down to actual drafting. So far they have been having what we would describe as a debate on the speech from the throne, without any actual work being done on the drafting of documents. For example, I think it is essential that as quickly as possible they start drafting terms of reference for the international supervisory commission, and also declarations, one of neutrality which it is planned would be signed by the 13 nations, apart from Laos, attending the conference, and a second declaration to be signed by Laos when agreement is reached as to the government of that very unhappy country.
The second objective was to outline in broad terms Canadian views on the terms of
reference for the truce supervisory commission. This commission, of course, is our main interest in the situation in Laos. It is because Canada is a member of that commission that she is attending this particular conference.
Then I had in mind also getting proper support for the truce supervisory commission in the way of more specific instructions and equipment.
Finally, I wanted to confer with the representatives of the other countries which are attending the conference. This I suggest is very important, because quite a bit can be accomplished by discussing the situation from time to time with all the other delegates no matter whether they are of our general point of view or not.
It might be helpful to those members of the house who are interested if the three statements which I made during my visit there could be printed as an appendix to Hansard. That would cut down the time required for me to make an adequate report to the house today.
With regard to the first objective, I am very hopeful that some time next week the conference will start to discuss in restricted session the terms of reference for the commission. The idea is that there should be perhaps two or three representatives of each country rather than the larger number who have been sitting in thus far, and that there will be discussions rather than a series of set speeches.
The plea for more support for the international commission met with quite wide approval from the other delegations. I made this plea on June 15. The following day the United States and France both submitted in writing to the co-chairmen of the conference, the United Kingdom and the Soviet union, offers of equipment. I should also like to have these offers printed, if I may.
The Soviet union as one of the co-chairmen must, of course, consent to any such support being given and Mr. Gromyko, the foreign minister, has been holding back on giving approval. He put forward the suggestion that the three member nations represented on the commission, India, Poland and Canada, should send messages to their commissioners in Laos asking if it would not be possible to get this equipment, particularly light airplanes and helicopters, from the Laotians themselves.

Report on Geneva Conference
That seemed to me to be a very foolish idea. However, we agreed to send a message to Mr. Leon Mayrand, our Canadian commissioner in Laos, asking for his views about the possibility of hiring from the Laotians the equipment necessary for the commission to do its job. We had a reply on Monday, June 19, and I think the house would be interested in reading that reply. It sets out very clearly just what obstacles the commission is facing in Laos because of the failure of the co-chairmen to supply adequate equipment. Incidentally when I criticize the cochairmen I am really criticizing the Soviet union, because all the way through the British have been prepared to have this equipment supplied but they alone cannot make the decision. It has to be a joint decision by the two co-chairmen. The Canadian reply from Laos was the only one which had been received when I left Geneva yesterday morning.
The day before yesterday I made a further statement dealing with the absolute necessity of supplying this equipment, and my statement was supported in a very helpful way by the representative of France and by Governor Averell Harriman, the rep-presentative of the United States, and by Right Hon. Malcolm Macdonald, the chairman of the British delegation, whose support was particularly important because he is one of the two co-chairmen of the conference.
In the meantime the three Laotian princes have been meeting in Zurich, Switzerland; Prince Boun Oum, premier of the government which has been recognized by the United States and Great Britain, Prince Soup-hanouvong, who is the head of the Pathet Lao and who is representing the communists, and Prince Souvanna Phouma, who is described as a neutralist. They apparently have been making some progress. There is an encouraging report this morning but it is in very general terms, and it would be unwise for the house to expect that any definite final agreement would be made among the three princes tomorrow, the next day or maybe for some time.
I am afraid that the Soviet union is not very anxious to have an effective commission in Laos. This is my judgment after listening to their remarks and noting their actions with regard to requests for equipment. One quite effective way of handicapping the commission is to fail to supply or to delay supplying the commission with what it needs in the way of equipment. That is not a very helpful process.
The task Canada has undertaken as a member of the truce supervisory commission is a very onerous one. The representatives of the Department of National Defence and the

Department of External Affairs in Laos are doing an excellent job under extremely difficult conditions. I think the work of the commission is exceedingly important. It might just be the means of preventing a third world war arising out of what is happening in that country in southeast Asia. In any event, the presence of the commission and the fact that the conference has been sitting in Geneva have, I am sure, greatly reduced the actual fighting in Laos. They have not stopped it altogether, but in my opinion there would have been much more fighting if the commission had not been set up and if the conference had not been held.
Canada will do what she can to help out. I am sure all hon. members of the house will support the Canadian delegation in their attempt to follow that course. We are very well represented. The chairman of our delegation is Chester A. Ronning, the Canadian high commissioner to India. He was born in China and speaks Chinese; in fact he attended school with one or two of the Chinese delegates, and is able to give great assistance in the deliberations at this conference. We also have Paul Bridle, our ambassador to Turkey, who served for a year as Canadian commissioner in Laos. A third member is Ralph Collins formally head of our far eastern division in Ottawa. Mr. Collins too was born in the Far East. We are also receiving excellent assistance from Brigadier George Leech of the Department of National Defence who has served on the Canadian commission for Viet Nam. These Canadians are working in Geneva in a situation which can in no sense be described as a holiday and, I believe, are rendering a great service to our country. I am glad to pay this tribute to them today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure I express what every member of this house wishes me to express at this moment when I observe that once again we are glad to welcome the Secretary of State for External Affairs back from an important international conference. The fact that we have done so at least three times since January, during this session, indicates the interdependent character of the world in

which we live and the importance of our country in the context of this contracted world.
We note with interest that the minister says he hopes there will be a drafting of the terms of reference of the international truce commission next week, and also that there will be some form of the kind of neutrality in the government of Laos which it is hoped to be able to achieve. The minister has cautioned us about being overenthusiastic about the statement of the three princes as reported in today's press. Nevertheless their statement indicates that some progress has been achieved toward some form of coalition. It is to be hoped that the kind of neutrality which will emerge will be an honest neutrality, not one that will represent a government that will play closer to the communist world than to the western world. We hope that it will be, in fact, as President Kennedy said, a neutral government. However, we have reasons for being concerned about the likelihood of this result in the future.
The minister should know that we fully support him in his desire to see that the international truce commission of which Canada is a member is given every protection and every assistance to maintain its security and render efficient its operations. However, we note with concern the statement of the minister that he is of the opinion that the Soviet union is not anxious to see an effective commission operate in Laos. This statement from the minister confirms our own apprehensions; but coming from him, with his knowledge of the situation, it gives us reason to be greatly concerned.
We can only hope that we shall be able to meet the reluctance of the Soviet union in this particular and that, to the extent that it is possible, we shall be able to provide conditions of relative peace in an area which, as he said, is so vital at this time if we are to avoid a conflict on a much wider front. If the Soviet union does not co-operate with the commission as one of the chairmen of that commission I hope that Canada as a member of the commission will not hesitate to say so and will not hesitate to take steps consistent with this reluctance of the Soviet union to give full effect to the terms of the commission.
May I finally say to the minister that while he was away dealing with the problems of peace and war, we were serenely engaged in this house with matters that were very peaceful.
Report on Geneva Conference

subsubtopic: REPORT ON GENEVA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of this group I wish to associate our members with the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East with respect to all of us being pleased to see the minister return safely home again. On behalf of our members I wish to thank him for his immediate report to this house on his latest mission. In doing so he shows for this house and this parliament a respect which has not always been shown in the past under similar circumstances. We give him full marks for that courtesy and for his very fair and, in our opinion, objective report.
I was also very glad to see that the hon. gentleman had the various statements and documents attached to today's Hansard as an appendix. This makes it very much easier for us to read them carefully and digest fully the results of his mission and the report he has given the house. I am glad to hear that the pleas on the part of the commission for more support met with a good response. I noticed that on reading some of the papers. That is a good sign. It shows there is a moral force behind this mission from persons of good intentions and good will.
I was also interested in the hon. gentleman's report with respect to the signs of progress, should I say, toward co-operation among the three princes involved. We must remember when we are dealing with circumstances like these, particularly with questions related to the Far East, that these people do not move as quickly as we do. We have to exercise a lot of patience. They do not think quite as we do. While at times it may be frustrating, I think the minister takes the right point of view when he indicates that there is hope of progress and co-operation in time. That depends to a great extent on the attitude of the members of the commission.
I was interested in the hon. gentleman's comment to the effect that the presence and actions of the commission had reduced the hazards of fighting in that area. Well, that is a major accomplishment in the first instance. All we have to do is imagine what could have been the circumstances without that commission and without the effective contribution made by the Canadian members on that commission.
Members of this group wish to join with others who have spoken in paying tribute to the excellent service being performed by Canada's representatives on the commission and in the related work for Canada and for the world as a whole. We pay tribute to them for the way they are performing what, as everyone must recognize, is a trying task.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be quite a tall order for me to add anything to suggestions made by Premier Khrushchev, as it is hard enough to find out what he is getting at without trying to help him out.
There is no meeting of four foreign ministers on the question of disarmament. What is going on is a conference between the United States, represented by Mr. McCloy, who is the head of their disarmament branch, and Mr. Zorin, representing the Soviet Union, who is a deputy foreign minister and permanent representative at the United Nations. They are discussing informally in Washington the type of forum in which disarmament negotiations could be resumed. They started to meet on June 19 and those talks are still going on. Therefore it is impossible for me to say what the decision will be. The plan was that disarmament negotiations proper should commence about August 1.
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis
With regard to the test ban conference in Geneva it, too, is still in existence. The leading United States representative has been recalled to Washington for talks. It is true that Premier Khrushchev has suggested that those talks should be merged with the talks on general disarmament which are supposed to take place about August 1. I believe the United States has rejected that suggestion, and I do not know what will happen with regard to that particular three-nation conference in Geneva. The third country represented, of course, is the United Kingdom.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Five. Well, Mr. Speaker, if I still have five minutes at my disposal, I am pleased.
Since I have five minutes left of the time which was allotted to me yesterday, I should like to make a wish concerning our friends opposite. I hope that today they will rise in greater number than yesterday to defend the miserable budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming).
Indeed, sir, last night's performance was not too impressive since only the Conservative members for Kingston (Mr. Allmark) and

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. McMillan for Dorchester (Mr. Drouin) participated in the budget debate whereas on this side, the members for Grand Falls (Mr. Granger), Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets), Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) and Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) and I took the floor to discuss the budget we are now considering.
Or course, Mr. Speaker, I realize that this year just as last year, the budget has not provided much to satisfy the hopes of our friends on the government side. I can understand that they are disappointed, disenchanted, distressed, disillusioned, desperate and discouraged, but I ask them to change their attitude today, because when things go wrong, it is not good politics for a party to show it to the public.
I suggest that more of our Conservative friends should rise today and cover up their great disappointment. I would particularly ask the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay)-who, I am told, is quite dissatisfied with the budget-to forget these things, come into the house and be as talkative on the occasion of the budget debate as he is when he interrupts the speeches of members of the opposition.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, when I spoke in the budget debate on January 16 last I made some remarks which I should like to quote. I refer to the last sentence of my remarks as reported at page 1095 of Hansard. I said in connection with the baby budget:
-I believe also that the different members of the cabinet should be helping the Minister of Finance in a department in which we have a continuing and chronic emergency.
The events which have taken place since that time would lead one to believe that there is something wrong with the Department of Finance. The minister has been convinced by somebody somewhere to change his thinking on interest rates. For some three years and half I have been telling this house that our interest rates are too high and that they were at the very root of our economic ills. In the windy and wordy budget speech the other night the Minister of Finance certainly gave lip service to this premise. I shall quote some of his words. At page 6645 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
To begin with, interest rates in Canada are out of line with those in the United States and some of the European capital-exporting countries.
This is something that we have been saying for at least three years and a half. I recall quoting the New York Times in the house

three years ago to the effect that interest rates in Canada were out of line with those in the western free world. At one time I quoted the interest rates on Cuban bonds in New York, and at that time I said the Diefenbaker bonds were selling lower than those of the Batista government and certainly lower than those of the Castro revolutionary government in the first three months it was in office.
At page 46 of the budgetary papers there is a table showing the long term government bonds yields. It also shows the differential between interest rates in Canada and in the United States. At the time of the election in June, 1957 the differential was about one half of 1 per cent. Later, in the fall of 1957, this differential went down to, I would say, three eighths of 1 per cent. This table has not been so prepared as to give the exact figure, but I would say it is about three eighths of 1 per cent. After the conversion loan and after further financing the differential got up to around 1J per cent. Since last year it has eased somewhat. It has again eased somewhat lately, and according to this table I would say it stands at about 1J per cent today. I say that the actions of this government in handling our fiscal policy and in the management of our debt have brought this about. Further down on page 6645 the minister said:
High interest rates are a double drag, at times like these, on our economic activity and expansion.
Still further on the minister said:
Statistics indicating trends of interest rates in recent years in Canada and abroad are to be found in the white paper. These support the view that Canadian interest rates have grown out of harmony with those abroad ...
That was not the story of the minister previously. As I said before, I have been bringing up this matter in the house for the last three and one half years but the minister has only seen the situation lately. He has only seen it after a good part of our debt has been built into a debt structure of long term non-callable bonds at high interest rates. In the meantime the provinces and the municipalities have assumed long term debts by way of bonds and debentures, and the taxpayers in the provinces and the municipalities will be paying these debts with high interest for years. Some of them will not mature for 30 years, and I am thinking particularly now of debentures on sewers.
High interest rates have also brought about stagnation in our economy. I could quote innumerable statements I have made in the past to the effect that high interest rates would increase taxes at all governmental levels, and we know they have done so. We on this side of the house said that

high interest rates would increase the cost of living, and they have. We have said that high interest rates would increase the cost of production and therefore make us less competitive in the markets of the world, and this they have done. We have also said that high interest rates would attract foreign capital to this country in order to earn a higher yield on such capital and that this would contribute to a greater imbalance in our international payments. This too has been brought about. The budget attempts to correct the effects of high interest rates which the government itself has brought about.
As I have said, I think interest rates are basic to our economic well-being. When you remove from the budget the measures taken by the government to correct its former mistakes with respect to interest rates you have not got much left. I admit there are two or three things in the budget of which we approve. The first is the removal of the excise tax on automobiles. The hon. member for Essex East has often urged this, as have other members on this side of the house. I also want to thank the minister for giving some consideration to volunteer firemen. I think I was the only member of the house who brought up this matter at the time of consideration of the resolutions following the baby budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Many members spoke to me about that.

At that time I asked the minister to exempt for income tax purposes at least $200 of the honorarium they receive. The minister has gone further and has set the amount at $300. I wish to thank the minister for that.
That is to allow for the inflation he expects.

Third, there is the provision, which I think will help the tobacco growers, by which more tobacco may be included in cigarettes. I hope the tobacco growers of western Ontario will get some relief and will be able to sell more tobacco. But when you take away from the budget the measures it contains to correct the mistakes of the government with respect to interest rates and the three other provisions I have just mentioned, there is absolutely nothing left in it. The budget contains little to cure our economic ills, including the imbalance in international payments of which interest rates have been the principal cause.
I am glad to see the minister give lip service to lower interest rates, but giving lip service to lower interest rates is not going to bring them about. The ordinary taxpayer will continue to pay high government taxes and in
The Budget

Mr. McMillan many cases high interest payments on bonds for the rest of his life. The taxpayers will continue to pay high interest rates for their share of every new school, every new sidewalk, road or sewer. Every new home owner will be called upon to pay high interest rates for a good many years to come.
Unfortunately the lip service given by the minister is no solution to those of us who have been caught up in the payment of high interest rates. I am glad that at this late date the minister has had a change of heart. It is something like a death bed confession, his last chance before wrecking our economy. Until his repentance he was the high priest of high interest rates in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

Why does he merit this appellation? In debt management, purely under the control of the minister and in no way the responsibility of the Bank of Canada, we have had the spectacle of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance appearing on radio and television and making statements in the press recommending that bondholders should take more interest on their bonds. They were told that it was in the national interest and was the patriotic thing to do.
I am referring, of course, to the conversion loan. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, on radio and television and through statements that appeared in the press, pleaded with and begged Canadians to convert their 3 per cent victory bonds into \\ per cent conversion loan bonds. They not only begged them to do so but they also paid them to do so. They paid every thousand dollar bondholder who converted to take $45 interest each year instead of $30 each year. At that time it did not make any difference to them whether interest rates in Canada got out of line with those in the rest of the world. At that time it did not matter whether interest rates were a double drag on our economy. It did not matter then if there was an increase in the imbalance of payments. It did not matter whether they caused stagnation in our economy. What mattered then was that the minister should be in charge of the greatest financial transaction that ever took place in Canada.
The minister continually required more money. To cover his deficits he had to continue to raise more money, and this caused an upward pressure on interest rates. It was not until early last year, when the country learned that the minister was going to budget for a surplus, that interest rates eased. In addition, the minister devised gimmicks for

The Budget-Mr. McMillan the benefit of the wealthy friends of the government. The government devised ways and means to give its wealthy friends some extra interest taxwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Untrue.

Deficit or no deficit, these people had to be looked after. When the government came to power in 1957 the average rate of interest on our debt stood at 2.98 per cent, slightly under 3 per cent. The minister and the Prime Minister in the bond conversion loan tried to get as many people as possible to increase that by 50 per cent, to change as many bonds as possible from 3 per cent victory bonds to 4-J per cent conversion loan bonds. For subsequent borrowings the minister paid much higher rates, as I said before, and the total interest payment on our debt has now increased by approximately 50 per cent. I suppose they have reached their goal and achieved their objective. Now comes the deathbed repentance.
By the end of this fiscal year the extra debt charges imposed on the taxpayers of Canada in the four years, including this year, will be $800 million. It is made up mostly of interest. The first time I or anyone in this country had any indication that the minister had a change of heart in connection with interest rates was on June 14 last, when something was brought up in connection with the resignation of Mr. Coyne. I would say that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance blazed a trail for high interest rates on our national debt. They have now attempted to cover up this fact by erecting a smokescreen. Heads must roll and so Mr. Coyne, governor of the Bank of Canada, is losing his head. It is quite within the realm of possibility that before long he will be blamed for the conversion loan.
Firing the governor and erecting a smokescreen will never conceal the damage the minister himself has caused. So much of our debt is built into high interest non-callable bonds. If money could be borrowed tomorrow at 3 per cent this government could do nothing about these bonds because they would not be callable. Therefore we could not reduce our interest on these bonds.
The former government, and I think a great many former governments, sold bonds that were callable so that in a low interest period these bonds might be called in, redeemed and reissued at a lower rate. I have always maintained that this government was a prisoner of its own mistake in that conversion loan. I predicted in this house that the government would never escape and it never will.
I predicted that it would grope around, and it has. I predicted that it would blame some-

one else, and it has. The government in terms of taxes has stamped itself on our country for a generation.
It is interesting to think of the capital projects that could have been undertaken with the $800 million of extra interest. For instance, that amount of money would have built two St. Lawrence seaway canals or five Welland canals, on the basis of the cost of constructing the latter canal at the time it was built. If capital works had been built the people would have had employment and something tangible they could look at, instead of being faced with increasingly high income tax rates. It would not be so bad if the $800 million could be paid and we could then be done with it, but that is not the case. That sum has gone to create new debt. This year, as in previous years, the government will not raise sufficient money to pay the interest on the $800 million, so we will continue as we have in the past, paying interest on the interest.
In discussing the budget the Minister of Finance often counters our criticism with the argument that we are bringing up the same old stuff. I would be the first to agree with the minister, because if we adhere closely to the budget we are indeed discussing the same old stuff. The minister does not vary the diet. He gives us bigger and bigger deficits and more and more debt. He increasingly demonstrates his ability to be further off the mark in his predictions in respect to budgetary figures. Fifteen months ago the minister reported that we would have a $12 million surplus for the last fiscal year. I predicted then that the deficit would be much more. In December the minister predicted that there would be a deficit of $286 million. At that time I said it could not help but be more. He came along in the last budget and said the deficit would be $345 million, I believe, and his prediction was off the mark by $1 million a day.
For the next fiscal year the minister predicts a deficit of $650 million. I cannot agree with that figure. In view of past experience I do not think anyone could say that the minister's prediction is likely to be at all close to the mark. I recall that the minister used to find fault with former Liberal ministers of finance because they were out in their budget predictions by approximately $50 million on the favourable side. I predict that the present minister will be out more than this amount on the unfavourable side of the budget. I should like to be wrong once in my predictions for the sake of the taxpayers of Canada, but this last budget has not changed our idea about

the dismal Diefenbaker day. We are certainly going to continue to be confronted by a $2 million a day deficit.
When the former Liberal government left office in June of 1957 there was a surplus of $400,000 a day. Today the deficit in connection with extra interest alone is more than half a million dollars a day. In addition to this, when the former government left office there was approximately $900 million in the unemployment insurance fund and approximately $200 million in the defence equipment account.
What has happened? In order to conform to the needs of the various assessments of our economy made by the Minister of Finance the defence equipment account was soon raided and is now nonexistent. The unemployment insurance fund is almost bankrupt, containing at this time only approximately $65 million to meet a depletion of about $300 million a year. The daily deficit on overspending on current account has piled up to the point where it now reaches an enormous sum. After the budget it will stand at over $2.2 billion.
Considering the overspending on current account together with the depletion in government accounts, it will be seen that this represents an amount of more than $3.3 billion, a colossal sum. This is more than twice the cost of world war I between the call-up of troops in 1914 and demobilization in 1919. Since it came to office this government has indulged in overspending in an amount more than twice the cost of world war I during the period I mentioned. Canada had over 500,000 troops overseas in those years, yet in less time than the length of that war this government has found it possible to overspend more than double the cost of the war with little or nothing to show for it. We have heard much about the minister being expansive in his budget. He was expansive only in debt, not in tax cuts. We would not complain about tax cuts of sizeable proportions if they were designed to put people to work, but this amounts to only $65 million in this current fiscal year. The minister expects the budget proposals to cause a rise in our tax collections to offset the $65 million in tax cuts, yet he is predicting a deficit of $650 million this year as against a surplus of $12 million predicted in his last budget. I was interested in another halfhearted prediction of the minister to be found at page 6665 of Hansard, which reads as follows:
On the basis of the present situation and anticipated trends it is not unreasonable to expect that the current flows of revenue and expenditures will be approaching a balance by the end of 1962. Indeed, as our economy reaches high levels of
The Budget-Mr. McMillan employment, it is essential that the budget should achieve a balance, and that provision should be made for an orderly retirement of debt.
All I can say is that on two occasions the minister has attempted to predict the result of the budget for just three months ahead and he has been out by upwards of three quarters of a million dollars a day in those predictions. Last year, as I said, when he predicted ahead for 12 months he was out by about $1 million a day. How much is he going to be out when he starts to predict ahead for 18 months?
In speaking on the budget then I referred to the fact that some orderly reduction should take place in the value of our Canadian dollar, as I thought it would help exporters in the country. But at that time, as we all recall, the minister said it would cost too much to buy United States money in order to do this, that it would mean a considerable expenditure of money. The thinking on this matter by the minister has also somersaulted, just as it has done in connection with interest rates.
On Wednesday evening I was quite interested to note that the Conservative party here celebrated the fourth anniversary of their assumption of office and responsibility for the direction of the affairs of our country. I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister and the members of the government on attaining four years of power. I could not, however, but feel uneasy that on the very day of this anniversary our dollar was plunging in the various markets of the world, and there was chaos in those markets. I do not mind admitting that I experienced some emotion on learning that branches of the various Canadian banks in such centres as Los Angeles, New York, London and Paris did not have enough confidence in the Canadian dollar to trade in it. I heard that statement over the radio and I have since read it in the press. What dealings took place in those centres were mostly between United States banks and British banks. I know this situation will clear away, but certainly there has been left some lack of confidence.
I was laughed at in this house when I predicted that unless this government changed its ways there would be some flight of capital from Canada. On August 10, 1960, as found at page 7914 of Hansard, I said this in the house:
Two years ago I predicted these high interest rates. I am afraid that If the minister carries on as he has been there will be flight from the Canadian dollar.
Then I went on to say that I did not know how much more the Canadian taxpayer could take but that certainly, if the next two years were anything like the last two, we would

The Budget-Mr. Winch see our currency depreciated. I should like to ask the members of this house what was going on in the last few days if it was not a flight from the Canadian dollar-a temporary flight, at least-in the various markets of the world. In fact I myself know some people who were hurrying to get their money out of Canada at that time, and trying to get the best deal they could in United States dollars.
I do not know whether this abrupt change or abrupt fall in the Canadian dollar has ever occurred previously. However, I appeal to the minister and to the government to have a more orderly change in the future. If it is desirable to have our money selling at some figure below par, 1 suggest that this should be done in an orderly way and not in the way in which it was done the other day.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am
sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I must inform him that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I was bitterly disappointed in the budget speech presented the other day by the Minister of Finance. After hearing, as we did, his vociferous emotionalism and oratory about the coming expansionist budget, I feel certain that all of us in this house as well as the people of Canada were really looking forward to a militant, progressive, constructive budget outlining policies, legislation and action which would aid to a considerable extent in curing the ills which have beset our Canadian economy in the past and still beset it. As I say, Mr. Speaker, I was bitterly disappointed because I did not see that much looked for expansionist policy.
But perhaps of even greater importance is the fact that I find the presentation made by the minister frustrating and confusing. It could not be anything but frustrating and confusing because almost in toto it was a tour de force lasting for over two and a half hours and consisting of cliches and platitudes and repetitions of cliches and platitudes. It was not what I think the members of this house and the people of Canada had a right to expect, namely a clear explanation of the basic and fundamental economics underlying the proposals which he made. I myself found it difficult to understand the basic economics. I believe the Minister of Finance owes it to this house to present a picture of the fundamental economics in such a way that there will be an understanding of why he has brought in the proposals contained in his budget speech.
May I say here also that I have been most disappointed in the fact that we have not heard from some of the backbenchers on the government side of the house. I have taken

it for granted that the Minister of Finance is a true believer in democratic methods and procedures and therefore that, in such an important matter as a budget, he would have taken all his backbenchers into his confidence and would have explained to them the economics of his proposals. If that procedure had been followed I would have thought the backbenchers would have an understanding of the economics and therefore, as one would gather from their applause for the Minister of Finance, would have been happy and proud to rise in their places and explain to the other backbenchers in this house and to their constituents the real and fundamental meaning of the economics of the budget.
I can only come to the conclusion that they also find the basic economics frustrating and confusing, and that the reason we have not heard from them is that they do not understand the matter and that it has not been explained to them. The situation is either that, Mr. Speaker, or the whip has really been cracked and they are under orders not to speak in the budget debate. As a matter of fact it is current in the corridors this morning that the whip has been cracked and that we shall not be hearing from the backbenchers. If that is so it is a peculiar expression of democratic procedure and a peculiar expression of Conservative back bench representation in this House of Commons. I hope we shall hear from some of them, because we should like some explanation.
It was interesting to note that when the Minister of Finance started he did not give us an analysis of the economic situation of Canada past and present, explaining from the position of government policy and administration what had gone wrong with our economy. No; it was something outside government, something outside Canada which had brought all these things to pass. Almost in his opening remarks the minister said, and I quote from page 6640 of Hansard:
Last December in presenting to the house a supplementary budget, I explained that the rate of economic expansion in Europe had shown some hesitation and that the economic outlook in the United States and Canada, which had been most encouraging at the beginning of 1960, had rather unexpectedly reversed itself, resulting in a disappointing slow down during the last three quarters of 1960.
So the failure of the government to succeed in its operations in Canada was because of what had taken place in the United Kingdom, in Europe and in the United States. I think that is a weak way in which to begin an expansionist budget and to explain away the mistakes and fallacies of the present government. However, it was not very long before we found that the Minister of Finance

had taken a second look. He put on his rosy glasses and told us that everything was going to be different in the future; because we also find on page 6640 these words attributed to the Minister of Finance:
Expansion is expected to continue in western Europe and in our other important overseas markets. These welcome developments will make possible further increases in our exports, production, employment and incomes. Thus, an improvement in our situation could be expected to occur even if no further efforts were taken to stimulate our economy.
Thus not only have the government's failures in the past been blamed on what was taking place in foreign countries, but now Canada is going to reach a new heaven because of what is taking place in other countries. I think that is a ridiculous way in which to introduce a budget and upon which to base government policy. Of course we all hope this new vision is not just something seen through rosy hued glasses. We hope the situation which the minister outlined is going to come about. But if it is, Mr. Speaker, that has got to be related to government policy and proposals as outlined in the speech of the Minister of Finance. I think the minister owes it to the house and to the people of Canada to explain just how his policies related to these other countries are going to bring about the desired result.
His economics are indeed most strange. The minister almost completely ignores all the fears which have been growing as to what is likely to be the effect on Canadian exports when we relate them to the expansion and the fulfilment of the plans, policies and purposes of the inner six and the outer seven. That, I think, cannot be explained away by the minister in the course of a casual mention. Neither can we accept without explanation the contention that his policy is going to mean a greater expansion in the export field. I refer in particular to the United Kingdom, although all our export markets come into the situation. We have to recognize this, and I do not know why we completely close our eyes to it. If you are going to export you have to import. If you are going to export, the countries to which you export have got to have Canadian dollars, and to have Canadian dollars they have to be able to get their exports into our country.
When you have a policy of devaluation of the dollar it is true that on the surface that is undoubtedly going to assist our exports, but how is that going to be counterbalanced by the fact that we have to get Canadian dollars in order to pay for our purchases from the countries to which we export. We have to import from them in order that they may get the Canadian dollars for our exports. By the devaluation of the dollar we are
The Budget-Mr. Winch without doubt, whether the minister wants to admit it or not, doing the same thing we would do by erecting higher tariff barriers. It means that we have to pay more dollars because our currency is being devalued.
I think it is stupid to talk, as the government is disposed to talk, about our rightful market in the United Kingdom, and to express our fears about the United Kingdom going in with the inner six; because we have to realize that Great Britain must think about her 48 million people, and that is her first concern; and that if we want to sell, as we do want to sell, more wheat or agricultural produce or lumber or pulp or paper or salmon or other fish to the United Kingdom, the United Kingdom has to be able in turn to export to Canada. Therefore we cannot consider in isolation the fact that the government policy of devaluing the dollar is going to help us with our exports. What is going to be the effect of the counterbalance if it is going to hurt us in regard to imports when we cannot get the Canadian dollars for the sale of our goods? Just what are the views of the minister on the counterbalance on the imbalance? What indeed? The minister did not tell us one word about that, and I say that is where he is being distinctly unfair. He only wants to show us one side of the picture, and if we are going to have a successful government and a successful policy we have to have both sides of the picture and we have to have a complete balance.
I do not think we have heard enough in the explanation given of the devaluation of the dollar as to what it is going to mean in Canada itself. As was pointed out in the question of the hon. member for Niagara Falls this morning, there is a certain impact which already has been felt.
It was the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillanj.

No, I am referring to the question about eating cake. If the reports in the press are correct the price of wheat has gone up. Because the price of wheat has gone up the price of flour has gone up, and because the price of flour has gone up the bakers say the price of bread is going up. So we are already feeling an impact. Now how is it going to affect other fields, other imports which are basic necessities in Canada? Let us take just a few small items in use in every home every day, whether it be tea or coffee or cocoa or spices, all those things which we shall now have to pay for with a devalued dollar. I think we are entitled to a better picture of the economic survey and analysis made by the minister so we may know just what this will mean as far as the cost of living in Canada is concerned.

The Budget-Mr. Winch
The minister is seeking to get the provinces and the municipalities to do more of their borrowing in Canada. That is a desirable objective. He hopes by his present policy to enable that money to be borrowed at lower interest rates. That is an objective with which we all agree, and we hope it saves the millions of dollars that the minister is looking for and anticipates. I should like to see this policy of economics carried all the way through, but the minister does not do that.
Of course we agree with the devaluation of the dollar and the stated objectives which we hope will follow, but what will be the cost on the other side of the picture, to the provinces and municipalities, which have to pay back hundreds of millions of dollars which they have borrowed in the United States and elsewhere, on the basis of that devaluated dollar? I suggest it will cost millions of dollars which the provinces and municipalities have not anticipated having to pay. How and to what extent is this going to be balanced? I suggest this involves some of the basic economics which have not been explained by the minister. I suggest that it is not fair to give only one side of the picture, and that to do so is to mislead the house and the people.
Mr. Speaker, as my time is moving on much faster than I anticipated I should like at this time to refer to one of the most important phases of the proposal of the Minister of Finance, which has not been referred to very much as yet. I refer to that portion of the minister's statement where he deals with dominion-provincial fiscal relations. I find his suggestion in this regard most disturbing. He has proposed that the tax rental system be discontinued on March 31, 1962. Mr. Speaker, I think I know something about this subject, because I was a member of the British Columbia legislature in 1941 when the first tax rental agreement was introduced. I was also there when this agreement was reaffirmed with changes five years later.
In 1941 the federal government asked the provinces of Canada to enter into a tax rental agreement. Why did the federal government do that? I suggest it was because of the necessity of the time for national planning and financing to meet the responsibilities of the national government in time of war. This necessity was recognized by the provinces at that time and they entered into agreements. peacetime, as there is still a need for planning and the solving of problems which must be overcome.

I feel this policy represents a serious departure from the path of progress which was laid out in 1941 toward national minimum standards. I suggest this new policy will renew the complications, duplications and inefficiencies in the taxation field. Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize the fact that I feel strongly about this matter of not only inviting but almost demanding that the provinces impose their own income taxes, because this policy is fraught with danger. I think we should recognize that without clear-cut leadership from Ottawa there is every possibility of a return, as I said earlier, to the tax jungles of the 1930's. Perhaps the most important result to the federal government will be the loss of its vestige of control over the use of income taxation as a means of combating unemployment and for stimulating economic growth. I can only envisage this proposal as an indication that from this time on the provinces and every individual in this country will be on their own.
I suggest all we have to do, Mr. Speaker, is to look back over the statements of the provincial premiers at the time of the October conferences, and the editorials which appeared in newspapers across this country at the time. I should like very briefly to refer to several of those editorials. In the Ottawa Citizen of October 26, 1960 there appeared an article under the heading, "Diefenbaker's Tax Proposals Stun Premiers". Premier T. C. Douglas has branded Prime Minister Diefenbaker's proposal to end the tax rental formula as a surrender to the wealthiest provinces and a "complete betrayal" of the others.

Offers Return to Tax Jungle". Let me quote two paragraphs from this article as follows:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker proposes to abandon the present tax rental agreements with the provinces and let them levy their own income, corporation and succession taxes.
This would be a double step backward. It would tend toward the Canadian tax jungle of the 1930's and it might easily promote national disunity by setting province against province, region against region.

Mr. Speaker, I want to indicate how strongly I feel in regard to this matter of dominion-provincial fiscal relations and agreements, mostly because of one statement contained in the minister's budget speech as found on page 6655 of Hansard of June 20, 1961, which reads as follows:
In short, it was proposed that the provinces would reassume their constitutional rights and responsibilities to impose and vary their tax levies as they saw fit.
I think that is the key to the minister's statement; he wants to return the constitutional rights and responsibilities to the provinces. I suggest that is entirely different, and an about face, to statements as I recall them made by the Prime Minister when he spoke in Massey hall during the 1957 election campaign. He said then that the provinces and municipalities could not discharge their constitutional responsibilities. Great as were the men and great as was their thinking at the time of confederation, they could not possibly conceive of the development of Canada and the development of new responsibilities of federal, provincial and municipal governments. The fathers of confederation had no idea of the development of Canadian democracy, whereby people looked to government as a right for health services, old age pensions, mothers' allowances, family allowances and unemployment insurance.
I suggest that this proposal of the government in this realm of federal-provincial fiscal
The Budget-Mr. Winch relations, with a return of constitutional responsibilities to the provinces, is unfortunately an intervention in that section of the British North America Act which deals with property and civil rights, which means basically employment and all those other social benefits which I have mentioned. I suggest a serious mistake is being made here, because the result will be that those social benefits, which were not contemplated at the time by the fathers of confederation, will disappear because the residual power will now rest in the hands of the provinces.
Despite the interpretation of governments or courts I say that is wrong. The residual power should belong to and be a responsibility of, the federal government, and there is a section which can place it there. I say it is absolutely impossible for the municipal and provincial governments to accept these new responsibilities because of the limit on their taxation powers. I say it is absolutely impossible to have a national minimum across Canada on account of the difference in the wealth, in the resources and in the productivity of the provinces. Surely we have to have that in effect in legislation and in policy if we are all going to be Canadian citizens. I say, sir, that the government is throwing all this overboard by returning to the procedures in existence prior to 1941. In particular, of course, this can be applied to that vast problem of unemployment.
I remember reading not long ago a statement of the premier of one of the provinces in which he outlined this feeling-and I agree with him-that widespread unemployment is obviously a problem in which all members of government share a common concern, but the predominant responsibility of the national government to launch corrective measures cannot be denied. It is the national government alone that possesses the strategic control over fiscal policy, and foreign trade, and the constitutional powers and financial resources which must be thrown into the battle against unemployment at all times.
Sir, this matter of dominion-provincial fiscal relations is one of the most important things that could come before the members of this House of Commons. It is a matter which strikes home deeply to every citizen of Canada. Certainly it strikes home deeply in so far as the provincial and municipal governments are concerned. I say, sir, this government is letting down the people and the provincial and municipal governments in setting the clock back in not only the proposals but in the demand that I understand has been made by this government, by the Prime Minister, upon the provinces that they shall have their-I think the term is "acceptance"-in by the end of September of this year. Hayden Stanton had the honour of representing my historic riding as a result of being elected in 1953 and re-elected in 1957 and 1958. To touch again on the matter of the bank and the Minister of Finance, it is difficult to address oneself to the merits as we have been permitted to hear only one side. However, I should like to refer to an article in the Economic Journal, being the quarterly journal of the Royal Economic Society. The editors were J. M. Keynes and T. H. McGregor. The article was printed in March, 1934. This goes back a long way, but let me read a few words set out in this learned article by a man esteemed by all banking authorities and a well known student of this subject, Dr. Clifford A. Curtis. The paragraph to which I should like to refer appears at page 54:
There can be no question that it is the duty of the central bank to stand out against the pressure of governmental policies which the bank believes to be injurious to the public good. But, if a government decides that a certain monetary policyusing the term in its broad sense-is desirable, and if it is prepared to follow it at all costs and to be responsible to the public for it, then it must be, under a democratic scheme of government, the duty of the central bank to carry out this policy. In an extreme case, the bank may appeal to the sovereignty of the people by making the matter at stake a public issue between it and the government. Such a possibility, however remote, is bound to exercise some restraint upon even headstrong administrations.
The fact, Mr. Speaker, that such an issue has developed is a crisis in Canada. The reasons for it are, perhaps, not as important as the fact that this particular thing has happened. I come to this house with great respect for all members of this house, and particularly those gentlemen who adorn the treasury benches. We know the Minister of Finance as a man of scholarship in the law, hardworking, dedicated, of an exemplary character, and so on. I believe that when the minister presented his budget in June of 1957, he meant exactly what he said. I refer to an article in the Toronto Star of June 26, 1957. This article bears the headline "Fleming's First Budget 'Tremendous Challenge' ", and reads in part as follows:
But Mr. Fleming says firmly that there will be a balanced budget.
I think that the distinguished minister intended precisely that. I compare that with the type of newspaper clipping we read today. The Toronto Telegram says:
In a startling reversal of his past position, Mr. Fleming has devalued the dollar.

The Budget-Mr. Matheson by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance. I should like, in the few minutes that are available to me, Mr. Speaker, to try to address myself to some of the things referred to in this budget. I would say this, that the minister can be characterized as an expansionist nationalist, whereas Mr. Coyne can probably be described as a restrictionist nationalist. Probably the only safe course at the present time is for Canada to pursue a policy that is more internationalist. I put to you, sir, that the minister puts faith in exchange manipulation. The word "manipulation" is entirely appropriate to what is happening, dealing with the symptom rather than the economic problem, thinking that by manipulation of the symptom he somehow or other is going to be able to change the course of economic fortunes in this country.
I think we can credit the fact, in the light of the minister's explanation during his appearance on television, that he wishes to frighten capital so that a change will occur immediately. This is an extraordinary development. His course on the import side is obviously restrictionist; it could have no other connotation. Indeed the hon. gentleman's policy as outlined in the budget, so far as exchange is concerned, is just as restrictive as Mr. Coyne's policy is with respect to tariffs. What are some of the foreseeable results of such a policy? It certainly is going to increase the cost of consumer goods. This morning we heard about increased bread prices, and other increases will rapidly follow. Increases in the cost of machinery will be another result. It does mean that, in fact, there will be a drag on new investment in Canada. The minister has explained to this house that this exchange manipulation may provide something in the nature of a stimulus to exports. However, this is exceedingly uncertain because many of our important exports in this country are exports which do not respond very rapidly to price changes. It does seem, according to the best economic advice available, that a good many of our markets in the United States are to large buyers who need our products and are going to take these products in spite of a slight price variation. There will be a response in price very quickly by Canadian exporters who, regardless of the kindly advice and warnings of the minister, will take advantage of conditions. The result of this will certainly be to move export and all prices up, to give larger profits where there have been adequate profits before. What possible advantage will flow from this? The ultimate results will be higher costs for the Canadian people.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is another very sinister aspect to this par-


ticular budget. This budget represents protection through depreciation. Some expansion is expected unless other countries catch on and retaliate. All we have to do is look back at the financial history of France and the United States, and particularly the morass into which Europe got itself in certain periods in the past, to realize how frightfully dangerous this course may be.
What about the international monetary fund? To what extent has Canada actually kept faith, to what extent is she now living up to her own exemplary record in the financial field? Moreover, such protection as is being afforded to certain people through this depreciation factor really means, if we analyse it at all, that Canadians hereafter must pay more for goods produced.
We are presently presented this choice, Mr. Speaker, in terms of achieving full employment. We can make the economy more efficient, and I submit that this budget does not do that, and does not address itself in any way to that problem. Alternatively, we can subsidize marginal industry by accepting a lower standard and that is the course of this particular administration. In so far as the exchange factor in this budget is concerned, certainly exchange depreciation rapidly destroys the competitive factor, the one thing on which Canadians should surely have concentrated their ingenuity in the last months and years. The exchange manipulation does not increase efficiency by one iota.
Let us look at it from another standpoint entirely. Up to now we have had a free exchange rate. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) has referred recently to his advocacy of private enterprise. Before this budget we have had a free exchange rate. What does that mean? It means an exchange rate determined by the play of day to day forces in the market-in the longer run by the position of our balance of payments. What about the alternatives, the fixed exchange rate which Canada enjoyed during the period from 1939 to 1950? This could work with certain advantages. A fixed exchange rate does give the trading community certainty about the rate. However, this government has given Canada neither. It has given Canada, if I may use the expression in a parliamentary sense, a bastard rate flexible but subject to political manipulation.
Now the minister gives us a manipulated rate influenced by market, by official action, that is the bank, and by the indecisiveness of the government itself. We have compounded on the natural laws of supply and demand the economic influence of the bank and the political influence of the government.

I put it to this house in earnestness that this is a dangerous and damaging thing to the future of this country.
How does the minister propose to "manipulate" the rate in the manner and to the extent he believes to be desirable? By the process of going into the market and buying United States dollars for which we need cash. Where are we going to get cash when we have an administration that, by its budget now, has piled up interest charges alone of something of the order of $200 million a year? Where are we going to go for the moneys that are going to be necessary to go into the market and buy these United States dollars? I submit that we have two alternatives. We are either going to borrow more or we are going to print more and neither is a very happy choice. We have to do one or the other.
I submit that this is an irresponsible act in another respect. We have had a policy declared with no action. What is the likely result of this announced policy? I submit that one of the first things we can look for is sharply increased United States investment in Canada-which I always thought was one of the things which the ministry side were very much against-but not United States investment in the sense of the past, not the establishment of some new industry and the earnest desire to build up, not speculative or risk taking at all, but rather such things as Americans buying Canadian homes, buying Canadian established businesses, buying what is already making a profit, buying stocks and so on and shares in Canada.
Can we not fairly say that the only result of this course-that is the Coyne-Fleming controversy-is victory for neither? No matter what the facts are, no matter what is presented to this house, there can be victory for no one. There can be only loss to all of Canada. When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) is being interviewed on television and elsewhere is being asked the question, "What would you do", I think there is only one proper answer. "No one else ever would have got into such a box." Have we ever heard of a situation in Canada where the head of the bank and the head of a ministry have worked so very badly together? Is this not part of a pattern-the decapitation policy of this government? Have we not seen this pattern develop with the loss of many extremely able people in Canada who were compelled to quit or who were fired?
This administration first came into power with tremendous fanfare. When we analyse the policy of the Prime Minister of Canada we find that he came into power in Canada with an approach that historically has had 90205-6-439

Speaking on the baby budget on January 24, 1961, as reported at page 1382 of Hansard of that date again I referred to the subject of the premium on the Canadian dollar:
The minister had nothing to say about the premium on the Canadian dollar. It is true that it is now at near par with the United States dollar. However, a stabilization of the rate of exchange for the Canadian dollar should be considered now. It should have been done a long time ago.
The apparent advantage of the premium has actually been a problem which interfered with the stimulation of export trade. I directed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the house during the trade commissioners' conference in Ottawa. I asked whether the high priced Canadian dollar had been discussed. I was more than mildly surprised to receive a negative reply from the minister whose responsibility it is to promote exports.
I venture to say that the minister of the newly created Department of Forestry-to whom I wish to express my congratulations upon his appointment, and also my best wishes-will not find it difficult to agree that the premium on the Canadian dollar has been a definite detriment to the forest industries, which are substantial in the economy of our nation. Were it not for a healthy pulp and paper business northwestern Ontario would be economically insolvent. I need not remind the minister that practically one third of our annual total exports is represented by pulp and paper, lumber and other forest products.
It is no secret, therefore, that in respect to lowering the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar I am in agreement with the program.
The plan of portable pensions merits the support of every hon. member in this house. Speaking on the vesting of pension rights, a subject which was introduced by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) on May 24, 1960, I had this to say as reported at page 4208 of Hansard of that date:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the discussion of this very important subject. I was interested in hearing the Minister of Finance state that portable pensions are not a matter of federal jurisdiction. I maintain, however, that the federal government has some responsibility in the matter of pensions and the provision of a general pension plan acceptable in every part of Canada. If that is the case, then it has got to be a federal proposition and not merely a matter of provincial jurisdiction.
One of the major problems facing workers in industry today is the difficulty of men over 40 getting another job if for some reason their previous job comes to an end. As everyone knows, the acceleration of technological change has hit the hardest at older workers who have been displaced by machines. Many of these displaced workers were participants in pension schemes of all kinds, as intimated by the Minister of Finance, but their prospects for security are threatened through loss of employment. As a result, people 45 years of age and over find it extremely difficult to get a job in industries that have their own pension plans which in many instances preclude the hiring of men and women over 40. The only fair solution to this problem, and it is a serious problem, is a measure or method, call it what you will, which would permit an employee to change his job without affecting his pension plan.

On March 16, 1961, as reported in Hansard at page 3033, I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) if he knew of a statement made by an official of his department to the effect that legislation on portable pensions would be introduced in the near future. The minister replied that he had been informed that the statement had no reference to federal legislation, but dealt only with the possibility of provincial legislation.
These and similar observations have been placed on the record by me regarding these three subjects, which should indicate that these desirable measures were not hatched in the fertile brain of the Minister of Finance who, after much prodding, came to the conclusion that suggestions made by members of the opposition have merit, after all. I will give him credit for a belated acknowledgment of their worth.
I also appreciate the minister's concern for the tobacco grower who he is going to help by allowing a fatter cigarette without an increase in tax. However, while he was thinking of cigarette smokers, I am surprised he did not give consideration to the users of soft drinks, chocolate products and toilet goods, because these commodities are of general universal consumption as are fruit and meats.
A budget designed to expand the Canadian economy should certainly contain a proposal for a municipal development bank from which municipalities could borrow for essential projects on long term and at rates o1 interest close to those which the federal government pays. This is, among other things, one of the striking omissions of this budget. The absence of such a fund has forced municipalities to borrow heavily in the United States money market to finance their local improvements, and these municipalities will have to repay their debts in United States funds which, with the devaluation of the dollar, will mean a substantial loss to them. Both these measures, the lowering of the value of the Canadian dollar and the establishment of a loan fund to help municipalities, should have been undertaken at least three or four years ago.

The municipalities are asking for access to capital funds at costs within their capacity to pay. In their importance as basic community needs many local improvements are of equal priority with those of the senior government. It would be only fair to enable municipal governments to have the same advantages as senior governments in respect of the capital market, and the only effective way to accomplish this desirable equity is to establish a municipal development fund or bank, call it what you will, to assist the municipalities, with the co-operation of the provinces, in borrowing for their needs.
The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities favours a federal agency which could be named the municipal development bank, the main function of which would be to purchase the bonds of a municipality subject to the approval of the province. The terms of such loans to the municipal governments would be as favourable as possible, consistent with the cost of the federal government's own borrowing. This would not eliminate the private investor who would still participate in municipal, financing, either by sharing in the initial underwriting or by purchasing bonds from the bank. A federal government guarantee of such securities would be as sound in principle as the federal government's guarantee of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I wish to submit another good reason for such a municipal loan bank within the jurisdiction of the federal government. The federal government has a triple role to play in coordinating capital expenditures, public and private, which come within the framework of the national economy as a whole. Such coordination would ensure a condition of steady growth and stability. At present I doubt whether the government can clearly see, let alone co-ordinate, the capital expenditures of the three levels of government. Over and above any other consideration, such a bank would certainly facilitate borrowing within Canada for Canadian needs. It would, therefore, be a positive means of implementing the federal government's policy of encouraging more reliance upon domestic savings.
The establishment of such a fund or bank would also remove the frustration and obstacles to development; it would give a sharp incentive to the forward planning of growth and redevelopment. It would also help to keep in each urban area a planned capital development program which, if implemented, would
The Budget-Mr. Badanai provide work and satisfaction in seeing the fulfilment of community needs.
At the lakehead we have a lakehead planning board, with a full-time capable planning engineer, whose plans are awaiting capital to transform the lakehead cities into a coordinated unit which would have the sure effect of attracting new industries and more people. I ask the minister to consider the suggestion of establishing such a bank at the earliest opportune time.
The Bladen royal commission report contains a recommendation which would have been of doubtful value in my opinion, had the government implemented it in the budget. I am referring to the 10 per cent duty on British cars which the commission has recommended. Today the United Kingdom is more and more under pressure to divert her trade to the European community. Such a tariff proposal would be just another obstacle to our maintaining our trade relations with Britain. If Britain chooses to join the European economic community we should then lose no time in allying ourselves with the same bloc. After all, Britain buys in round figures $1 billion worth of commodities in Canada, while our purchases in that country do not give Britain a favourable trade balance. These are factors-
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?

Let me finish. At the conclusion of my remarks I will answer any question the hon. member wishes to ask.
These are factors which command the attention of the government to a degree which has seldom been necessary in the past. In this budget the Minister of Finance has endeavoured to create the impression that he is providing Canada with a planned deficit in order to stimulate the economy. In reality the deficit that the minister will incur this year will be the result of an increase in expenditures based on departmental estimates that were drawn up as early as September of last year, and which had very little to do with the recession or its cure because unfortunately at that time the government did not recognize that the economy was suffering from a recession which caused wholesale unemployment.
In the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, this budget can only be assessed in terms of whether or not it contains solutions to three of Canada's principal economic problems, first, unemployment; second, balance of payments; and, third, economic growth.
With regard to the solution of the unemployment problem, there is little in the budget to tackle effectively this basic trouble. There

The Budget-Mr. Badanai is little or no support for the vocational retraining program established recently on a federal-provincial basis.
The Minister of Finance cannot put everything in his budget, but at the present time it is almost inexcusable to overlook support for a program upon which the government has placed so much emphasis. One might even wonder how sincere the government is in its sponsorship of this vocational retraining program when in the budget it grants tax relief to volunteer firemen but nothing is granted by way of tax concessions to those who undertake the vocational retraining program which is being done largely on a voluntary basis, or for that matter to those who are trying to educate themselves or their children at their own expense.
With regard to tax concessions granted in the budget for research, there will be little increase in the amount of research done by Canadian firms. A more positive incentive must be provided. If research is to be effectively stimulated something like a double tax credit will have to be given for expenditures for research.
The minister proposes to raise the tariff on textiles coming into Canada. These will come largely from Britain, Japan, India and Italy with which usually we have a favourable balance of trade.
