My question relates to the imbalance of trade with the United Kingdom. The hon. member said that exports from Britain to Canada were far greater than our exports to that country.
No, it was the other way around. Our exports to Britain are greater than our imports from Britain.

Yes, that is correct as to the total figure. Has the hon. member the figure for per capita trade with the United Kingdom and is he aware that it is greatly in excess of the per capita trade with Canada?
The hon. member has asked a question that I should try to-
Take it as notice and answer in due course.

Great Britain has approximately 50 million people and Canada has


about 18 million. If you wish to establish that figure, all you have to do is to use your pen or pencil and you will have it right away.
Would the hon. member answer the question? Is he aware that exports per capita from Canada are far in excess of imports from the United Kingdom on a per capita basis?

I presume that some members on the government side will undoubtedly take part in this debate and I sincerely trust that the hon. member who has asked me this question will make a speech before the end of the debate. I think it would be in the interests of all concerned for as many members as possible to rise from their seats and speak on the budget.
They would sound much better than your speech.

Inasmuch as I have been asked these questions, I should like to quote from an editorial in the Fort William Times-Journal of Wednesday, June 21, which seems to sum up the general reaction to the budget in these words:
No doubt a host of Canadians feel disappointed with the budget brought down in the House of Commons last evening. Finance minister Fleming may have provided the right nourishment for an ailing economy. But the menu is nothing like the fare which many had led themselves to expect.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I was trying to look around the house to see whether the friends of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) would rise at last to extol his budget and explain how beneficial were the provisions announced therein, according to him.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that we shall begin by having some order here, and if hon. members do not want to listen, let them go out. They did not speak last night. There was not a single Conservative member who rose to compliment or defend the Minister of Finance. They left him high and dry, and he is quite small.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke spoke.

I hope I did not insult the minister when I said that he is quite small, because I did not say it with any bad intent.
Mr. Speaker, last Tuesday night, we heard the Minister of Finance make his budget speech. It was the fifth budget of the Conservative administration and the second one for this fiscal year. He wanted-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was the first for this fiscal year.

I am sorry, the minister is right, it was the second in the fiscal year 1960-1961. Anyway, the minister took three hours to make that speech which, according to him should pull the Canadian economy out of its present stagnation. Well, after all the fuss of the last few weeks and the unusual delay in explaining the government's financial policies, the Canadian people, as I said last Tuesday night on television, was expecting a sensational budget. However, all the sensation contained in that budget was a deficit which will certainly this year exceed $700 million. The minister himself predicts that the deficit will be between $600 and $700 million but if we take the inaccuracy of his former predictions into account, we might easily expect a deficit varying between $700 million and $1 billion, an amount which is a far cry from the promises made by the Prime Minister at a press conference in Saskatoon on May 27, 1957, when he stated that the Progressive Conservative government would fulfil all its promises and reduce unnecessary taxes while balancing his budget.
And now, does the minister contradict this? Did the Prime Minister not say these words in Saskatoon?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was a good speech.

It now becomes evident, Mr. Speaker, more particularly after this fifth budget speech, that the Conservative government, in this field as in all others, has proved itself incompetent. Far from having succeeded, even on a single occasion, in balancing revenues and expenditures. It has the sad distinction of having reached a peacetime high in this respect for the last five years. The total of its five consecutive deficits reaches the phenomenal figure of more than $2 billion. That deficit-
(Text):
Did you hear your leader on the radio last night? He approves of a deficit.
The aggregate deficit incurred since 1957 exceeds $2 billion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A deficit of $2 billion this year?

Since 1957 the total deficit under a Conservative administration has reached a figure of over $2 billion. That is the budgetary deficit.
(Translation):
This record breaking deficit of $650 million which is forecast for the current fiscal year
The Budget-Mr. Bourget will bring the Canadian taxpayers no general income tax reduction nor will it cut down substantially the extremely high level of unemployment.
In fact, in his budget speech, the Minister of Finance did not foresee more than a 3 per cent rise in the national income, that is only a little better than in 1960, which was a recession year. In that connection, Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I read an article which was published in the Wednesday, June 21 issue of the Le Soleil. I should like to quote a paragraph from that article:
Mr. Fleming's speech mentions imports and exports. It also deals with several other important matters. It is based mainly on the expectation of an increase in the national product and income, but does not include anything likely to bring about an increase greater that could normally be expected. Indeed, it is a document lacking in dynamism. Short of a miracle happening from the outside, Canada must be content to mark time while seeing its national debt increase without being able to do anything about it.	-
That article gives us an idea of what independent people think of the present budget and of the results that can be expected from it.
At the outset of his remarks last Tuesday night, the Minister of Finance mentioned that every budget he has introduced since the Conservative party came into power was intended to answer current financial and fiscal problems. He added that this budget is designed to meet the present needs and difficulties of our country. "Flexibility, he said, has been the keynote of our financial policy in these four years."
Well, Mr. Speaker, allow me to say that besides having visions, the Conservative party now has delusions.
Indeed, one does not have to be an expert to understand that the measures enacted by the Conservative party since 1957, far from answering present problems, have only contributed to cause an economic stagnation.
After having been in power for four years, it seems obvious that the Conservative government is unable to correct the situation.
In June 1957 and March 1958, the people of Canada no doubt thought that they had elected people who could better look after the country's economy. Now, let us take a quick glance at what happened since the Diefenbaker team took over the administration.
Before I proceed, however, I think I should remind the house that when things are going badly in some sector of the economy, the Conservatives never miss a chance to imply

The Budget-Mr. Bourget that all that is due to the legacy we left them. What legacy did we leave them in June 1957?
A $260 million surplus. A national debt reduced by $2.5 billion. An unemployment insurance fund of more than $900 million. Trade agreements with the United States from which the Canadian uranium industry was deriving revenues of $300 million.
In October 1957, according to statistical reports, only 3.4 per cent of the labour force was unemployed.
As a matter of fact, when the Liberals handed over the administration, the nation's business was in good order and Canada's prestige abroad was very high. Today, after four years of Conservative administration, what is the situation?
I said a moment ago that, under the last year of the Liberal administration, there was a surplus of $260 million, and that, from 1946 to 1957, we had succeeded in reducing the debt by $2.5 billion.
Well, let us see what use was made of such a legacy. During the 1957 fall session, the Diefenbaker government, foreseeing undoubtedly the general election of March 1958, reduced taxes by a total of $204 million and increased social security payments-excepting naturally family allowances-by an amount of $115 or $120 million. But subsequently, that is in the April 1959 budget, the people of Canada were soon to find out that the Prime Minister had forgotten his promises for that year, taxes were increased by $352 million. Moreover, contributions from the workers to the unemployment insurance fund were raised 30 to 50 per cent, which meant a further tax increase of $75 million. If we add this amount to the $352 million mentioned earlier, we find that taxes which were reduced in 1957 by $204 million, were increased in 1959 by $427 million.
In short, that means that the tax reductions granted in December 1957 did not last very long and that we had to pay a high price for the increases in social security payments.
We would have had a right to expect that those new taxes would ensure subsequent balanced budgets; but far from it, all the budgets submitted by the Tory government since 1957, far from being balanced budgets, showed deficits totalling over $2 billion.
Deficits are a tradition with the Tories as is well known. Since confederation, that is since 1867, in all the years that they were

in power, and that means 43 years, there were only four years when the Conservatives succeeded in bringing down a surplus budget.
Should I also remind the hon. members of the colossal mistake made by this Conservative administration when in September 1958 it launched its famous conversion loan of $5.6 billion, the effects of which are still with us and the result of which has been to upset our whole economy.
We all remember that only a few months after this loan operation, the bonds lost from 12 to 18 points in value, with heavy losses for those who had to sell unmatured bonds. We remember also that money became tighter, which sent interest rates to an unprecedented level and deprived our industrialists, especially the smaller ones, as well as our businessmen of the funds required for modernization and development.
Our municipalities and school boards were also strongly affected by that situation, because when they were in need of money to carry out works that were absolutely necessary, they had to pay an interest rate which was often higher than 7.5 per cent. Needless to add that such an increase in interest rates meant for all our citizens an increase in municipal and school taxes for years to come. And, incidentally, do you know that since the Conservatives have been in power in Ottawa, the increase in the debt interest only has now reached more than $556 million?
It seems to me those arguments should suffice to show that the fiscal policy of the Conservatives has been a fiasco.
Have the results achieved by the Diefenbaker government been better in the field of federal-provincial relations? We still recall the promises made by the Prime Minister in that connection, among others, the one he made at St. Patrice de Beaurivage, in the constituency of my hon. friend from Lot-biniere (Mr. O'Hurley), on May 30, 1957, which is as follows:
Everyone admits that the relations between Ottawa and the provinces are bad and that they are unsatisfactory to both provincial governments and municipalities. The federal government is rich, but the provinces and the municipalities are poor and cannot go on assuming their obligations.
To summarize the attitude of our party, I repeat what X said when I opened the election campaign; we guarantee the provinces and municipalities a greater share of the tax dollar. We shall thus provide the provincial governments with the possibility of fulfilling their important constitutional responsibilities and of promoting the development of our natural resources.

Now, what has happened since then? Are the provinces and municipalities in a better financial position? Is it easier for them today to discharge their important constitutional responsibilities?
I say no, because at the fiscal conference last February, the government greatly disappointed most of the provinces. The federal government consented to very minor concessions in the field of the personal income tax. All it makes a pretence of giving the provinces in direct taxation it takes back immediately by changing the basis of equalization payments. Thus is sabotaged the formula for a fair redistribution of the national revenue the St. Laurent government had developed and called equalization.
After the last fiscal conference of February, the province of Quebec realized that there is nothing it can gain with the new proposals, that it will proportionally get nothing more than it did under the last agreement.
After the marvellous promises of the Conservatives in the elections of 1957 and 1958, our provinces were not expecting such a stab in the back. Therefore, the Conservative government must be held responsible for the unfavourable position in which it places the provinces as regards their future expansion.
I have here a statement made by the late premier of the province of Quebec, Hon. Paul Sauve, who had this to say in the fall of 1959, in a speech to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association:
We have reached the limit and unless there is a more equitable distribution of fields of taxation between Ottawa and the provinces, there is nothing left to be done. If the federal authorities do not realize that in 1962, I cannot see-
That was a speech by the then premier of Quebec, who was not a Liberal:
If the federal authorities do not realize that in 1962, I cannot see how confederation can continue to operate.
Neither must we forget, that, because of its numerous deficits and its many loans, the government runs the risk of dangerously exhausting sources of credit where the provinces and municipalities can find the capital they need.
It is therefore a mistake to contend that these new agreements will help the provinces to expand and develop.
Let us now look at the results of those steps taken by the Conservative government with regard to employment.
I said earlier today that in October 1957, 3.4 per cent of the entire labour force was 90205-6-440
The Budget-Mr. Bourget unemployed. Yet it can be remembered how the Conservatives, when they were sitting on this side of the house, criticized the Liberal government of the day. Well, if we take the trouble to look into the figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics, we find that the yearly average number of unemployed under Liberal administration was as follows:
In 1953, 3 per cent; in 1954, 4.6 per cent; in 1955, 4.4 per cent; in 1956, 3.4 per cent.
Let us now take a look at the statistics under the Conservative administration. I shall skip 1957, because the government was Liberal for one half of that year and Conservative during the other half:
In 1958, 7.1 per cent; in 1959, 6 per cent; in 1960, 7 per cent.
It can, therefore, clearly be seen that under the Conservatives unemployment has considerably increased. Yet, people still remember the famous statement of the Prime Minister who said, "no one will suffer as long as I am Prime Minister".
Well, again in this field, and especially in this one, the Conservatives have failed to find the required solutions to this situation, because at no time since they have come to power have we seen so many unemployed in this country.
In February this year, Mr. Speaker, there were 727,000 unemployed Canadians, or about 11.2 per cent of the total labour force. The government now seems to find some satisfaction in saying there are only 457,000 unemployed. They do not need much to be comforted, for it must be realized that this figure of 457,000 represents 7 per cent of this country's labour force, as well as 38,000 more than at this time last year.
The most deplorable thing is that the Prime Minister and his ministers have been denying during all these last few years that such a situation was abnormal. They merely said that that situation would disappear with the snow or with the coming of spring.
The only measure, I must make haste, Mr. Speaker, the only measure which was adopted to remedy the situation was the establishment of a winter works program which called for a federal contribution of only 12 per cent, the rest being assumed by the provinces and the municipalities. Perhaps the government will decide to put into practice the "bread and games" plan suggested by the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) or perhaps will they say, as they

The Budget

Mr. Bourget did before, that it is now up to employers and labourers to solve the problem because apparently the government has taken all the steps they feel they can take.
In short, that is a very sad inventory of the Conservative administration during the last four years.
The Minister of Finance has stated that the budget he has just presented is an expansionist budget. It is indeed an expansionist budget if, by that, he means that it increases the deficits we have had since the present government took power in 1957.
This is what he said to justify his deficit:
(Text):
In times like the present, a substantial budget deficit can promote economic expansion, with more jobs and better living standards for many thousands of Canadians.
(Translation):
In recent years, as I said a moment ago, we have had huge deficits. Hon. members will agree that in spite of that we have had a record number of unemployed and alarming spells of depression.
Since December 1957, Mr. Speaker, we have become used to hearing the Minister of Finance make optimistic predictions in the high sounding statements of his budget speeches. But at the end of the fiscal year, we always found that the government's financial proposals contained in the budget had in fact restricted our economic activities and had been utterly inadequate as far as increasing the production and volume of employment was concerned, as required for our expansion.
The speech delivered Tuesday night is only slightly different from the others. This is why it is a disappointment to the great majority of the Canadian people, and it can be concluded from the silence of our hon. friends on the government side that they are also disappointed with the deficit.
May I put a question to the hon. member?

Mr. Speaker, I have always been willing to answer questions, but considering that since last night hon. members opposite did not have the courage to rise in order to defend their own budget, they have no right to ask questions.
You are a coward. You are a coward just like your leader.

Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is very interesting to hear this exchange, Mr. Speaker, and also to note that the Conservatives must now make their contributions by way of questions to the opposition. This seems to me to be a surprising way of presenting contributions to any budget debate.
We shall show by our vote.
Sit down.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We have all watched what has happened during the past few months and it is very seldom that the backbenchers call a vote which the cabinet does not stand up and demand first. So we do not even get their opinion by the vote. They are probably getting to be better sheep than the Liberals were who preceded them in following the leaders.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: We were not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Maybe you were not, but that was the suggestion made at various times.
I think the Canadian people must have been very unhappy after this budget was presented. For days and days they had listened to an argument between Mr. Coyne as head of the Bank of Canada and the hon. member for Eglinton as Minister of Finance. They had heard them carry on a duel by letter and by remote control. They had come to the conclusion, I am sure, after the day long debate which took place in this house, that there was a difference of opinion. However, after listening to the minister's two and a half hour performance the other night I think the Canadian public came to the conclusion that there was very little difference in the positions taken by those two men. This is as it should be, since they are both Conservative economic advisers trained in very much the same school.
Ever since 1957 the Canadian public has been faced with an increasing amount of deficit budgeting. Previously, many Conservatives-and I am sure the minister himself was one of them-had felt that a budget in order to be a satisfactory budget should at least be balanced, and that the only reason for a deficit was the need to overcome some definite national emergency. I believe the

Canadian people held the view that the only reason for incurring a deficit, either in government finances or in their own personal finances, was when a need arose to acquire something urgently for which it was neither convenient nor possible to pay immediately; in any case, there was some reason that argued against saving the money in advance. I believe that during the war, especially, the Canadian people were willing to see large deficit budgets introduced because they knew exactly why such budgets were necessary. After listening to the minister speak for two and a half hours the other night I believe many Canadians are going to wonder just what this particular deficit is for.
It seems to me that if a worker got into the habit of going down to the finance company at the end of the week and borrowing $10 to pay his grocery bill and the other current expenses of his household it would not be long before the finance company would begin to take a serious view of his carrying on on that basis. Certainly there are credit unions-and I think it is true that credit unions probably take more interest in the welfare of their borrowers than do some other agencies-which would call the borrower in after making a few loans of this type and suggest to him that it would be to his advantage to borrow money only when he intended to use it to solve a particular problem. I think the Canadian people would go along with a deficit budget if the government could show that they are planning to spend more money than is immediately available to them only for the purpose of dealing with the economic recession and embarking on an employment program for Canadian citizens. But I believe we must look at this budget very closely if we are to find any evidence that either of these problems is being tackled with sufficient imagination and energy.
I think the country will also be concerned about the statements which the minister made about the relation of our economy to conditions in the United Kingdom, the United States and some other countries in Europe. He said these nations are experiencing an upturn in their economy and that this in turn will be reflected to the benefit of the Canadian people. This is probably true but it is certainly no justification for incurring a deficit in this country. That deficit is not helping us to solve our particular problem.
The C.C.F. party moved an amendment which stated in part:
-and this house regrets that adequate consideration has not been given and the government has failed to undertake social and economic planning necessary to stimulate the economy, provide full employment, and give an adequate level of social security by such specific measures as:
90205-6-440J
The Budget-Mr. Peters
1.	Raising basic exemptions under the Income Tax Act.
2.	Increasing old age security and assistance payments.
The reason we have suggested this basic increase in the exemption granted to small wage earners is that the money will flow immediately into the purchase of manufactured goods and agricultural commodities. We believe similar beneficial results will follow an increase in old age security and assistance payments. Such increases would restore the original purchasing power of the payments. In addition, an increase in family allowances would in large part, through spending by the medium and lower income groups, return to the federal government to the tune of 33 per cent in taxation. It seems to me that these are places where some assistance could immediately be given back to the people.
It is my belief that this government has not told the Canadian people the whole story of the financial conditions which are facing us. I believe that if the whole story were really told it would probably become known that the unemployment insurance fund had been a much greater factor than anything else in stabilizing the economy in very serious circumstances. Had we not had the $900 million reserve nor the payments that have been made to the unemployment insurance fund, there should have been a great deal less consumer goods purchased in this country because a vast number of unemployed would be without money. I agree that this program has put money into the economy of this country and reduced to a great extent the impact of the recession that we have been through.
While it is true that these increases will put money into circulation almost immediately, it is also necessary for the government to provide employment immediately. I suggest one way of doing this, and I congratulate the Minister of Public Works in this regard, is to provide money for housing at times when private industry is not interested in doing so. The amount of money which was supplied through the Department of Public Works in this regard has done a great deal to alleviate the situation. I believe a similar policy should be followed in regard to providing money for municipal capital expenditure, as well as money for capital expenditures on the part of this government.
I was surprised to note, in the highlights of this budget, the number of things which are supposed to be of value in comparison with what has been suggested in a number of statements made by Mr. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada. I agree that some of his statements have been made in regard to subjects outside the realm of his jurisdiction, and

The Budget-Mr. Peters a few of them have been made in a way with which the Minister of Finance did not agree. However, it has been generally conceded that a great deal of money being saved in Canada is being put into banks and other savings institutions, which should be reinvested in the national development of Canadian resources. There is very little difference of opinion as to how this should be done. The methods which are now being used are similar to those methods suggested by the governor on previous occasions.
I should like to ask a question, although I do not expect to receive an answer immediately. The fact that none of the Conservative backbenchers has spoken in regard to this budget I suggest is an indication that they have been directed to stand pat and not try to sell this budget, because it is impossible to sell unless the salesman possesses the extensive knowledge possessed by the Minister of Finance and his capable parliamentary secretary. Unless one does possess that ability and knowledge it is probably unwise, particularly for backbenchers, to try to show the value contained in this budget to their own constituencies because they are liable to muck the whole thing up.
In the choice of a new governor for the Bank of Canada I hope consideration will be given to the development that has taken place in respect to other banks in Canada, particularly with relation to consumer credit. The present governor of the Bank of Canada has had a great deal to say in this regard. He has suggested, as many Conservative backbenchers and others who support that party have said, that we should not spend more money than we have, and that it is not a good idea to live beyond our means. I believe that philosophy is followed by most Conservative finance experts and supporters.
Mr. Coyne has insisted that the 6 per cent interest rate be maintained. This has been a source of aggravation to the administrations of other federal lending legislation. The leader of the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has suggested on many occasions in this house that the limit on interest should be set at 6 per cent maximum in relation to loans made under federal legislation. He has introduced bills in this regard which have been talked out before even reaching a vote.
The head of one of the chartered banks in Canada has been suggested as a possible replacement for the present governor of the Bank of Canada. I should like to point out that the bank of which he is in charge has developed a small loans branch in competition with the finance companies. It is my understanding that the rate of interest charged, while not as high as the interest rate charged

by finance companies, which I understand is as high as 28 per cent, on occasion reaches 11 per cent, including the normal legitimate charges allowed. I should like to ask if the gentleman in charge of this type of activity is the type of individual this government is considering as a replacement for the present governor of the Bank of Canada? If that is the case then I suggest it is a good indication of the fact that there is a real difference in opinion between the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, will the hon. member permit a question? Would he recommend the president of a credit union for this position? The rate charged by those organizations is even higher, at 12 per cent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That subject could lead to a long detailed discussion in which I do not intend to engage at this time. I should only like to state that I have been a member of different credit unions and have always understood that loans from those institutions have always been made at the rate of interest of 1 per cent per month on the unpaid balance, which amounts to just slightly over 6 per cent. Hon. members may argue that is just slightly under 12 per cent, but I am not prepared to take up that subject at this stage. If I am wrong and the interest rate amounts to 12 per cent then I suggest the Bank of Nova Scotia small loans branch is charging twice that rate, perhaps as high as 22 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Such nonsense.
Why do you not get the facts instead of talking nonsense off the top of your head like that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have just said that I am not prepared to argue that subject. I have just suggested that the Bank of Nova Scotia, which the Minister of Finance seems happy and anxious to defend, makes loans charging an interest rate as high as 11 per cent. If the calculation made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) is correct, then I suggest the interest rate charged by that bank is perhaps twice what I understand it to be.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

It is not many years ago that portable pensions were unheard of. I can remember when the subject was first discussed in the mining areas. Miners were working for many years in the mines. Sometimes they retired at an early age. Sometimes they lived to retire at a normal pensionable age, and faced the fact that there was no money, no funds, no pension plan for them. Their position was exceedingly aggravated by the fact that in most instances they knew they could not have earned their living in their employable lifetime in any one particular mine because the mines did not exist that long. To be employed in the mine the miner had to be young and healthy and by the time he reached 60, 62 or 63, mines would have closed down and he would have had 10 or 12 years employment in one mine, maybe 15 in a second mine and a further period in a third. The miner had no opportunity to have a pension plan. The miners were also concerned with those very few places where a pension plan was in effect but the mines used that entirely as a weapon not for the employee but against him. They kept the employees in low-paying jobs; they told them if they did not like it to quit and obviously they would lose whatever pension they had accumulated. Usually they did not have a strong organization to speak for them and when they approached retirement age they were retired and did not receive any benefit from the fund.
Therefore our experience in northern Ontario has been a very poor one in relation to pensions. I can safely say that with the exception of the Sudbury area where the employees have had a longer mining experience in one mine, there have been very limited and very unsatisfactory pension arrangements throughout the whole mining industry.

Mr. Speaker, the presentation of a national budget is a very important matter. In fact, it is one of the most important items of business that come before parliament at any session. A budget is meant to serve two main purposes. In the first place, it affords the government an opportunity to give to parliament and to the Canadian people an account of their

national housekeeping and of their stewardship. In the second place, it affords the government an opportunity to make a statement with regard to changes in fiscal and monetary policies, with respect to current economic problems and also with respect to anticipated changes in future economic conditions. Incidentally, the budget can also be used as a political instrument to promote and advance party interests. I feel that it is in some ways a sad commentary on our political maturity both as parliamentarians and as a people that this aspect of the budget, which is rather incidental, should in some cases assume sufficient importance to overshadow its two primary purposes which I have just mentioned.
It is true, I think, from what we hear over the radio and read in the press that the greatest interest in the national budget stems from curiosity with respect to whether or not it will indicate an early election. I believe that the times in which we are now living are too serious to permit this kind of indulgence because the economic strength of our nation is an important factor in our national survival and I think we should look upon the Department of Finance in the same light as we regard the Department of National Defence.
The role of the opposition as I understand it is to examine the government's stewardship during the past fiscal year and that must be done, of course, in the light of last year's budget objectives. The opposition must also examine the proposed changes and these must be examined in the light of current problems and objectives. In presenting the national balance sheet and an account of the government's stewardship, the minister should remember that he is reporting not only to parliament but also to all the people of Canada and the people should be treated as fully grown and mature adults who are mature enough to face facts even though they may be unpleasant and who are willing and able to take whatever steps may be required by way of correction no matter how drastic those measures might be.
To accomplish that, these facts of the national budget, the national housekeeping, should be stated briefly, clearly and simply in language which can be understood by the average man in the street. That does not require a document like the minister presented on Tuesday, a document so lengthy and so verbose that it took him nearly 2| hours to read it. I might add that he read it very rapidly. If he had not done so, I am sure he would have taken well over three hours, which would have been another record of some kind or another.

He said: It gives me a great deal of pleasure to move the second reading of this Bill No. C-36 to provide for the establishment of a hospital sweepstakes board which would be empowered to operate a national hospital sweepstake. As hon. members know, there are some limits to the type of bill which a private member can introduce in this house, but it is my feeling that of all the bills which could be introduced by myself as a private member this one would be supported with the greatest degree of unanimity by my constituents and by Canadians in general.
I	think it is recognized that the people of Canada do want a national hospital sweepstake, and I should like to deal with some of the evidence in support of this contention. First of all, I would turn to the Gallup poll which has in recent years become a well known indicator of public opinion and the results of which have in most instances proved very accurate. The last time the Gallup poll questioned the people of Canada on this subject was in 1955 and the organization released the following statement on September 14 of that year:
There can be no doubt that a large majority of Canadians would like to see legalized lotteries and sweepstakes in this country. Even among the minority who disapprove, the largest number would change their opinion if the government were to run a lottery to raise money for health and welfare. Moreover, this feeling has persisted for a good many years.
The statement goes on to indicate that the question was asked: "Suppose the government operated a big national lottery to raise money for health and welfare; would you approve or disapprove?" Eighty two per cent of the people who were questioned answered "yes" to that question. I think that is a substantial indication that the people of Canada want a national hospital sweepstake.
It is interesting to look at some of the news stories which have appeared in recent years. I have here a number of photostatic
Sweepstakes
copies of news clippings which were kindly forwarded to me by the Vancouver Sun and the Vancouver Province after I had requested them to let me have copies of relevant items they had carried in their columns. Throughout, a great many bodies and organizations have advocated sweepstakes in this country including provincial legislatures. One dispatch from the Canadian Press in 1938 indicates that a resolution requesting the dominion government to legalize the operation of a sweepstake in the province to benefit hospitals was passed by the Ontario legislature by a vote of 48 to 34. Here we have a provincial legislature on the record, a good many years ago, expressing support for this proposal and there is a clear indication that since that time public opinion has swung further in favour of a national hospital sweepstake.
I have another clipping concerning Ontario. It is undated, but it is a United Press dispatch indicating that the Ontario municipal association has forwarded a resolution to the provincial government calling for lotteries to support hospitals. Here is the case of another substantial body supporting action of this sort. Then in 1954, according to a C.P. dispatch dated Ottawa, March 18 of that year, a further request was made for such a lottery. In this instance the request came from the unions. The cutting reads:
The trades and labour congress of Canada has repeated demands for a government sponsored lottery. The 580,000 member labour organization suggested an amendment to the Criminal Code allowing the federal government to set up a national lottery.
Here again is a substantial body on record as being in favour of a national sweepstake.
Another which appealed to me particularly is dated June 17, 1958 and is headed: "City Tories ask Legal Sweepstake". It reads:
Vancouver-Kingsway Progressive Conservative association favours a national legal sweepstake.
The article goes on to indicate that the association had asked the member for Vancouver-Kingsway to present its resolution to the federal government.
I have another cutting dated January 28, 1950 with the heading: "Vets Want Legal Lottery". The dateline is New Westminster.
An amendment to the Criminal Code to allow lotteries and raffles to be conducted in Canada providing all proceeds except necessary expenses be made available for charitable or/and benevolent purposes was requested in a resolution passed unanimously at the 27th provincial conference of the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans in Canada held here Friday.
I think that is sufficient to indicate that there is large and varied support for a national hospital sweepstake in Canada. The position of Quebec is, of course, well known in this regard. Some years ago the province passed its own lotteries law, but because it

Uruguay-lottery is under official control in Uruguay and is considered a source of revenue.

Only a state lottery may he considered an acceptable minor form of gambling but this again depends upon prevailing cultural patterns. General public opinion in Latin America does not consider such a state lottery as gambling.
I have been given figures on the Turkish national lottery. Unfortunately I have not had the opportunity to change them into percentages; therefore I will give the figures for the Turkish lottery for one year, and indicate how the money is brought in and distributed in the lottery. The distribution was as follows: The total revenue was 63,931,435 Turkish liras. The prizes paid out amounted to 32,417,795; commission given to sales agents amounted to 3,310,372; general expenses, 900,572. The net profit was 27,302,695. This will indicate quite clearly, Mr. Speaker, that the administrative expenses are comparatively low for the operation of sweepstakes.
The following information I have taken from the official year book of New South Wales, 1957:
State lotteries
State lotteries are conducted in New South Wales in terms of the state lotteries act, 1930. The act is administered by a director, and the lotteries are conducted on the cash-prize system.
The article goes on to indicate how the prizes are distributed and it appears to be operating quite satisfactorily.
My next information is from the year book of the commonwealth of Australia, 1958. It mentions the New South Wales state lotteries and indicates that the net proceeds of the lottery are paid to the consolidated revenue fund from which grants are made to hospitals. The Tattersalls lotteries in Tasmania have been going on for some time, and there again the money is paid into the hospitals and charities fund and the mental hospitals funds in such proportions as the treasurer determines from time to time.
In Queensland, the golden casket art union commenced in 1918 with the specific object of augmenting the funds of the Queensland war council. Since 1920 the net profits have been paid to the department of health and home affairs for the maintenance of hospitals, motherhood and child welfare trust funds, and so on.
In western Australia, lotteries are conducted by the lotteries commission under the lotteries control act of 1932. Profits are paid by the commission to hospitals and other charities.

Here again I might give the house some percentages so that an indication may be had of how effective and efficient lotteries in general are. These figures are for the golden casket art union of Queensland. I shall give just the figures for the year 1956-57. Amount of prize money paid out was 63.82 per cent; administration costs, 6.71 per cent; state stamp duty, 5 per cent; department of health and home affairs, 24.47 per cent. There again, Mr. Speaker, is a clear indication that the administration expense is not high in regard to the amount of money taken in.
I should now like to deal with the letter that I have received from the Mexican embassy indicating the value that sweepstakes have had in that country. It reads:
The national lottery for public welfare, of Mexico, is a federal government agency under the general authority of the department of health and public welfare.
Farther down it goes on to say:
The net proceedings are turned over to the department of health and public welfare for the construction and maintenance of hospitals, orphanages, clinics, etc.
The national lottery has been in existence for 90 years, and has performed a most meritorious work with complete public support.
I should now like to refer to an article which appeared in the Financial Post of October 10, 1959 entitled:
They Pay for Culture By Robson Black
Hon. President, Canadian-Scandinavian foundation
Sweden finances most of her culture by a chain of public lotteries. This may be "gambling" but in no sense does the system employ professional gamblers. Indeed, few countries in the world suppress with such a zeal all commercial games of chance, barbotte dens, cardsharps and roulette wheels.
Lotteries, however, are legal fund-raisers, all of them tightly supervised by government accountants.
The embassy of the Republic of China has given me the following breakdown of the distribution of their lotteries: 10 per cent to dealers as commission; 40 per cent as premium; 40 per cent as profit; 10 per cent for tax and administrative expenses.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, and give the details of a good many sweepstakes and lotteries operated throughout the world, but I think I have given sufficient indication to support the view that not only the vast majority of Canadians are in favour of a national hospital sweepstake but no harm is seen throughout the world in the operation of a government-operated sweepstake.
It was rather interesting to note in the Ottawa Citizen of January 16, 1959 that this matter came before the board of the United church. I found it somewhat amusing. This statement is contained in the middle of the

article. I do not want to delay the passage of this bill and therefore I will not read the whole article. It reads in part:

''What can I do?" he asked.
"I tried to say 'You'll go to the devil,' but they say they're having a good time."
Dr. Mutchmor advised him to seek action by the local United church conferences.
Finally, I say it is quite clear that there is a substantial amount of money going out of Canada. As has been mentioned, it is hard to get a proper estimate, but in the annals of the American academy of political and social sciences a couple of years ago- I do not have the exact reference here-it was estimated at that time that between $100 million and $200 million was going out of Canada each year to buy foreign sweepstake tickets. I firmly believe that we cannot stop the people of Canada from buying sweepstake tickets if they want to buy them. They have indicated quite clearly that they do want to buy them and it is the responsiblity of this parliament, if the democratic process is to operate properly, to carry out the wishes of the people of this country and institute at once a national hospital sweepstakes.

This committee conducted hearings for three years. I well remember the representations made before that committee and I know the final decision of the committee was in opposition to lotteries. I do not agree with that decision. I cannot agree, either, with my seatmate, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Begier). I just cannot believe he is so naive as is indicated in the way he spoke.
Let us look at the matter intelligently and from a psychological point of view. The majority of the people of Canada, whether it is right or wrong, moral or immoral, legal or illegal, are imbued with a sense of gambling. You are not going to change that by passing a law. This has been proven time after time in Canada. As a matter of fact, sir, I still remember that the people from whom we got the opposition were the top brass of certain organizations, and some of their own people ran some of the biggest gambling establishments in Canada. I say this because gambling is not limited to horse racing. Raffles are a form of gambling. I challenge, yes even my seatmate, to show me a political organization, fraternal organization or religious organization that does not conduct raffles. Raffles, as I said, are a form of gambling. I challenge anyone to show me a religious or fraternal organization that does not run a bingo. As a matter of fact, the biggest bingo operation in Canada-we had proof of it in our committee-was run in Ontario and Quebec by fraternal and religious organizations.
Raffles, bingo, horse racing, sweepstakes are all forms of gambling. There is a certain

instinct for this in our people, and I am afraid we are not going to be able to control it by passing a law. Whether we like it or not, millions upon millions of dollars are going out of Canada to the Irish sweepstakes, the United Kingdom football pools, the Australian sweepstakes and the Mexican sweepstakes. My hon. friend now mentions the Kentucky derby. You may control many things by law, but I am afraid you are not going to remove the inherent idea people have that they may get something, not for nothing, but for the purchase of a raffle ticket, a sweepstake ticket, a pool ticket or something else.
If we are going to be completely honest, surely we must ask: why not have some of this money stay in Canada to be used for social purposes in this country? I say, therefore, that in principle, because I think I know people and I think I have the evidence, I am in support of this bill and I believe it should be adopted.

Mr. Chairman and distinguished delegates:
This afternoon I should like to make a very brief speech concerning the effectiveness of the international commission for supervision and control.
As you are all aware, Canada's main interest in this whole Laos question arises through the fact that we were named as a member of this commission.
When I spoke here four weeks ago on May 18, I emphasized the vital importance of providing the commission with the essential technical means to supervise the cease fire and to report on the effectiveness of that cease fire. There was general agreement with these views and the co-chairmen sent a message, on May 19, asking the commission to inform them of requirements for the exercise of its functions in relation to the cease fire. I should have expected that by now, some four weeks later, the necessary equipment would have been provided.
The commission has submitted six reports from which it is evident that, while there has been no general renewal of hostilities, there have been a number of infractions of the cease fire, the most serious of which was the recent outbreak of hostilities at Ban Padong.
So far the commission has been unable to report on these violations from first hand observation. In their message to the commission on June 12, the co-chairmen referred to the commission's intention to discuss with the parties in Laos-now I am quoting from the message of the co-chairmen-"proposals for making the cease fire more effective" and the co-chairmen called on those parties in Laos, the three parties in Laos to co-operate with the commission in its task of supervising and controlling a cease fire.
But I must draw attention to the fact that even if that co-operation is forthcoming in Laos, as I hope it will be, the commission lacks its own means to move to areas of reported conflict and to inform the co-chairmen and the conference.
As the representative of France said on May 31-and I am quoting from that statement-"So far the commission which has its headquarters at Vientiane, has not been able to go anywhere else but Xieng Khouang,
and to do that it had to borrow a French aircraft which happened to be there".
In other words, this commission is not being given a fair chance to do its job. And to do that, it had to borrow a French aircraft which happened to be there. Why should this commission have to go around borrowing a French aircraft, or other equipment, in order to do its work? I suggest that this is putting an imposible onus on the commission.
More than six weeks ago the commission, in a report to the co-chairmen dated May 1, stated-and I am quoting now from a report to the commission from the co-chairmen -"The commission should be able to set up an effective machinery provided"-provided-"that the co-chairmen were willing to supply the commission with an adequate number of airplanes and helicopters, together with facilities for their maintenance".
That was six weeks ago. Three weeks ago, on May 22, in reply to the inquiry from the co-chairmen dated May 19, the commission said that its minimum requirement of helicopters was six and of aircraft, six. I submit that it would be a reasonable step-and I know we all want to be reasonable-without waiting for further word from the commission, for this conference to make available immediately at least three light aircraft and three helicopters and the personnel for their operation and maintenance.
It is perfectly clear, Mr. Chairman, that, if it were the will of this conference to provide the technical resources the commission requires, these could be immediately obtained from a variety of sources. In other words, this is not a case where it is impossible to get equipment. The equipment can be obtained, if the will is there, and the responsibility, I suggest with all deference, is on the two co-chairmen.
I therefore ask that the co-chairmen arrange without further delay to make these and other essential requirements available.
In this way the conference can insure that the commission is properly equipped to perform its immediate tasks, and, in so doing, can facilitate the work of this conference on other issues. And I hope to offer comment on these issues early next week.
But surely it is a test of the willingness of this conference to get some results. A very

good test is whether or not this commission- which after all has to do the work out in Laos of supervising the cease Are-the test is whether this commission can be given the equipment to do that work, and given it right away, without any further delay. And I do suggest that action be taken in order to bring about this result.
Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS AT GENEVA CONFERENCE ON LAOS, JUNE 19, 1961

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
I listened with great interest to the statement by the distinguished representative of Burma and if I may be permitted to say so, I thought he made a very helpful contribution to the deliberations of this conference.
My own purpose today is to state Canadian views on the aims and principles of a settlement in Laos. But before discussing the details of such a settlement, I would remind the representatives here of the high expectations and hopes which the people of my country- indeed people everywhere-have of the conference. Today, of all the international conferences concerned with the peaceful settlement of important international disputes, this conference, by general consent, is the one that holds the greatest promise of constructive results. After all, we start with the advantage that all the parties to the conference are agreed on the main aim-a sovereign, independent and neutral Laos. This aim was explicitly endorsed by the President of the United States and the Premier of the Soviet union in Vienna. If we are to fail, the implications for peace would be far reaching. Therefore we here are concerned not only with Laos, but with the hopes of mankind for an orderly settlement of disputes and the future peace of the world.
We cannot, I suggest, disappoint world opinion. I suggest that the time has come for the conference to end general plenary discussions and begin consideration of the details of a settlement. Certain specific proposals have already been laid before the conference by the French and Soviet delegations. There are also the agreements on Laos of the Geneva conference of 1954, which are bound to be the foundation upon which any Laotian settlement now or in the future can be built.
As a first step I suggest that an article by article tabulation should be prepared of the French and Soviet proposals, setting comparable articles in parallel columns, alongside the relevant articles of the Geneva agreements of 1954, in order to focus the attention of the conference on specific topics and to serve as an initial basis of discussion. Such a
tabulation could be prepared by the co-chairmen's staff or by some working group, but I think it is an essential first step in an orderly approach to our work.
The conference in restricted session, not plenary session but in restricted session where free discussion rather than set speeches would be the rule, should then take up article by article the various parts of a Laotian settlement on the basis of this comparative tabulation. This discussion would proceed in sequence from topic to topic in order to reach as much of a common view as possible.
For instance, if we start with the functions and terms of reference of the international commission, we shall have to deal at some stage or other with the subject of the commission investigations. For discussion of this subject we would probably have before us article 7 of the Soviet draft terms for the international commission for supervision and control, article 6 of the French draft protocol on control, and article 30 of the cease fire agreement of 1954. In each of these there is already a high proportion of common language, and the differences which exist might well be narrowed by discussion in restricted session. Other delegations could propose their own version for improving the text or reconciling divergent views.
Then at that stage a drafting group might meet to work out a single agreed text. By adopting a procedure along these lines the conference could hasten a settlement in Laos. And I have in mind that a similar procedure would be followed with each of the topics.
I now turn to an outline of Canadian views on what should be included in a settlement. There will, of course, be declarations on the neutrality of Laos to be made by the government of Laos and by other governments represented here and we appreciate that such declarations are of great importance.
Canadian views on what a Laotian settlement should contain are based on our service, over many years, on the international commissions in Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam. Therefore I confine my remarks today mainly to those parts of the settlement which especially concern the international commission. With this experience in mind, my delegation wants to see the terms of reference of the international commission so worded as to enable it to do a useful job.
I am convinced, that in framing terms of reference as part of the present settlement, we should take as our starting point the cease fire agreement of 1954 modifying it only as has proven necessary in the light of experience and of course taking account of changed conditions. The terms of reference are like a well thumbed book of rules which

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
have gained a certain authority and meaning by virtue of constant use. On the other hand, experience has shown that they were in some respects inadequate for the duties and responsibilities placed upon the commission in the past and they may not be wholly appropriate for the changed circumstances facing the commission in 1961. In the interests, however, of preserving those articles which have stood the test of time, I think it would be wise if the conference were to frame the relevant provisions of the new settlement as a protocol to the 1954 agreement on the cessation of hostilities in Laos.
Then a few words about relations with the government of Laos. We start, as I have already said, from a common position that the settlement should ensure a truly neutral, independent and sovereign Laos. Moreover, it is generally agreed that responsibility for the government of that country must rest with the Laotians themselves.
Let me make it perfectly clear that we have no desire to see the international commission interfere with the normal exercise of sovereignty by the government of Laos. Canada has no wish to see established in that country a commission which would have the slightest resemblance to what some have characterized as a super state. We look to a state of mutual confidence and co-operation between the commission and the government of Laos. We think this is vital and we are in full sympathy with the natural desire of the Laotian leaders to run their own affairs. Indeed, it is precisely to protect Laotian sovereignty that the commission is undertaking its duties of supervising a settlement in Laos.
However, if the international commission is to be an effective instrument of this conference in carrying out the terms of settlement, the responsibilities of the commission must be so defined as to enable it to perform its tasks. In this connection it must be recognized that the commission cannot function if it is made answerable at almost every step to some other authority and can act only at the request or with the agreement of such authority, for example the co-chairmen. Perhaps they could bear that in mind.
To avoid unnecessary friction and misunderstanding between the Laotian government and the commission, it is also important that the terms of reference should spell out with some precision the rights of the commission to obtain necessary information, both documentary and on the ground. To give an example, experience on international commissions suggest that it would be essential for the commission to be able to inspect
aircraft and to have access to manifests, in order to control the importation of war material.
Then a few words about the initial responsibilities of the international commission. While fully recognizing and welcoming the responsibility which the government of Laos will assume for its own affairs, the conference will obviously have to include in the settlement, provisions covering the steps to be taken in the military field in the early stages on such questions as the identification and withdrawal of foreign military personnel. Due account also will have to be taken of any formal cease fire agreement which is worked out in Laos. Arms which may have been brought in from outside will have to be collected and disposed of in some suitable way. The forces now opposing each other in Laos will have to be sorted out as a preliminary to the formation of Laotian security forces. All these matters, particularly the formation of Laotian forces will, of course, primarily be the responsibility of the government of Laos. The international commission, however, will have to accept some responsibilities, on behalf of this conference, for supervising these processes. This kind of activity by the commission will be essential for the establishment of a neutral and stable Laos.
Then there are the continuing responsibilities of the commission. The problems I have just been discussing are of a transitional nature. The main problems, however, with which the commission will be concerned will be of a more continuing nature. For example, it will have to assume responsibility in connection with preventing the re-entry of foreign military personnel; ensuring that armaments are not imported in excess of a level appropriate for the requirements of the reorganized Laotian security forces and taking other steps which may be necessary with respect to the security of the Laotian state.
I think we can assume that the commission will have some responsibility with respect to threats to the security of the Laotian state. Such threats obviously can originate either within or without the territory of Laos iself, or represent a combination of the two. In view of the general acceptance by all members of this conference that our primary concern is with the creation and maintenance of the conditions necessary for an independent and neutral Laos, and not with the internal affairs of Laos as such, the commission's responsibilities in this field will have to be very clearly defined.
And then freedom of movement. One of the facilities which the commission will certainly need if it is to assist the government

of Laos in ensuring that the provisions of the settlement are properly implemented is freedom of movement and freedom of access, where necessary to the effective discharge of its assigned tasks. And here I must register a complaint that just a few days ago the commission was refused by the Pathet Lao permission to visit Ban Padong which is the one place in Laos at the present time which in my opinion would justify a visit by the commission. But certainly within the last four or five or six days, the Pathet Lao has refused to allow the commission to go to Ban Padong. The commission will also need to have the co-operation of the Laotian authorities in providing protection for its personnel.
There can, I think, be no doubt that because the commission will have responsibility for safeguarding Laotian neutrality and independence through supervision of the entry of foreign military equipment and personnel, it must establish an adequate number of teams for this purpose. The number and location of commission teams should be sufficient to include all likely points of entry. If this conference should decide to make specific provision for the team structure, as was done in the 1954 agreement, it is important that provision be made at the same time for the commission to adjust this structure in the light of experience. Alternatively, the conference may wish to leave the question of number and location of teams for determination by the commission itself in consultation with the government of Laos.
Intimately related to the responsibilities mentioned above is co-operation by the government of Laos in furnishing periodic returns on the strength of the Laotian security forces. This is necessary to enable the commission to confirm that agreed force levels are not being exceeded and that military or paramilitary units are not being formed or maintained which might constitute a threat to the security of the Laotian state.
Then I come to the question of voting in the commission. Most countries represented here have expressed the view that the 1954 agreement should form the basis of a Laotian settlement. I have been very surprised to note, however, that some of the documents tabled contain provisions which depart radically in principle from those in the present agreement. The important question of voting in the commission is one outstanding example. Under the present agreement, decisions are taken by majority vote on all matters except three: first, violations or threats of violations which might lead to a resumption of hostilities; second, amendments to the agreement; and third, reduction of the activities of the commission To suggest that all
matters except purely procedural questions should now be decided unanimously is to depart completely from the Geneva agreement and would I submit make the commission utterly ineffective.
We who have served on the commission have had a good deal of experience with the voting procedure adopted in the present agreement, and I believe from what he has said in this conference that my Indian colleague, Mr. Menon, would support me when I say that this procedure has on the whole worked very well. It involves a striving for unanimous decisions whenever possible, but leaves the way open for majority action when this is necessary. I for my part, would resist any derogation from the existing provisions of the 1954 agreement in the direction of enforced unanimity.
Voting procedure in the commission is in many ways closely related to the manner in which investigations by the commission are handled in practice. And now I come to the question of investigations. I must confess that I am unable to see any justification for the double veto which has been suggested in one of the proposals before this conference. I am referring to the veto involved in the proposal for unanimity in the commission and the further veto contained in the proposal that investigations by the commission related to the introduction of foreign military personnel should be undertaken only on instructions from the two co-chairmen. I suggest that the two co-chairmen are getting a bit too high and mighty if they expect to have this power. This second restriction would deprive the commission of any initiative in its task of assisting the government of Laos to prevent the entry of foreign military personnel or to ensure the carrying out of the provisions of a settlement. We think that investigations should be undertaken by the commission either on its own initiative or at the request of the government of Laos.
It would seem highly desirable that the terms of reference should provide for regular reports at suitable intervals from the commission to the members of the conference. That, I am afraid, has not been the practice followed in the past with regard to these commissions and I presume Canada is as much to blame for that as any other country. Such reports would, of course, not in any way prejudice the obligation of the commission to keep the members of the conference informed of any serious situations which may arise, through the medium of special reports indicating whatever remedial measures might be considered appropriate. In addition, it is my view, that if the commission fails to reach

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
unanimity on a report, it should submit majority and minority reports and, when necessary-when no two members of the commission can agree-it should have the authority to submit separate reports.
I should also like here to mention a special aspect of the problem of guaranteeing that adequate and suitable equipment be made available to the commission to enable it to carry out its task. I am sure my views on this general subject are by now well known, but I emphasize again that the terms of reference should specify that all equipment which it may require will be placed at the disposal of the commission, and that such equipment will be fully under the commission's control. This is a subject on which we suggest that the two co-chairmen of this conference must take action. It has been dillydallying on it long enough and now when a proposal is put forward that the members of the commission should try to beg, borrow and steal equipment from the Laotians themselves in Laos, this I suggest is going to a ridiculous extreme and it puts the members of the commission in an impossible position. To this end, the conference will also have to make provision for the funds necessary for the commission's operations. At the present time, India has agreed to advance I think the sum of two hundred thousand dollars but so far as I know there has been no thought given in this conference whatever to the financing and India is just holding the bag and I do repeat that this question of financing is a vital one which has to be faced by every delegation attending this conference.
There is a final point which the conference will have to take into consideration. This is the eventual termination of the commission's activities. Whatever arrangements are agreed upon by this conference, it is, I think, important that the commission itself be given the discretion to recommend when it considers it is no longer required. In addition, of course, the commission should have the capacity to adjust the scale of its operations as circumstances warrant.
I conclude, Mr. Chairman, by stressing again the urgent need for this conference to organize itself in such a way as to make steady and orderly progress toward agreement on specific texts. The urgent need now is to create a momentum toward agreement. This conference has been sitting for nearly five weeks. While we were not sitting for the first three or four days-the distinguished delegates will remember we were all hanging around waiting to start

but we have actually been sitting five weeks tomorrow and there is not much to record in the way of results and as I said the conference has not even
settled the simple matter of basic equipment for the commission, to which I shall have to refer again at another time.
Canada, as I have emphasized, approaches the problems of the conference from the point of view of trying to help a country to achieve neutrality, stability and genuine independence-to help an unfortunate country which has been torn by internal strife and subjected to external pressures. All that we ask of this conference is support for the commission in Laos and more rapid progress -much more rapid progress-towards an agreement which will put an end to the tragic situation in that unhappy country.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On June 15 I raised the matter of equipment for the international commission in Laos and proposed that three aircraft and three helicopters be made available immediately. The following day, on June 16, the co-chairmen received offers of equipment from the governments of France and United States. These offers were contained in letters to the co-chairmen from the two delegations which have now been circulated as conference documents. You will note that these offers include three helicopters for the use of the commission as well as light aircraft, and the French offer includes the personnel to operate this and other equipment.
On the same day the two co-chairmen, however, met and came up with the idea, if I may use a colloquialism, which was communicated to me, that each member nation of the commission should separately inquire of its commissioner in Laos, whether the equipment might be made available by the parties in Laos, in other words, by Laotians. At the time, I found this notion strange, to say the least, in the light of the two unanimous requests-I repeat, unanimous requests-for equipment that had already been made by the commission and of the offers that had been received. However, in the hope that it would hasten action by the co-chairmen, I agreed to send a message to the Canadian commissioner in Laos asking him whether adequate transport and other requirements could be provided by the Laotian parties. I have now received Mr. Mayrand's reply, Mr. Chairman, which is available for distribution if it is so desired.
Because of the situation in Laos, the commission has had to accept severe limitations in practice on its right and duty to carry out investigations of breaches of the cease fire. As you know, there has been a failure of the

parties to give their agreement to such investigations, particularly on the part of the Pathet Lao, despite messages from the cochairmen urging the parties in Laos to cooperate; and despite also the unanimous decision, again by the three members of the commission that certain specified sensitive areas should be visited.
The results in Laos speak for themselves. In seven weeks of operation the commission has been unable to make a single on-site investigation of any alleged violation of the cease fire, even, as I stated on June 19, of the serious incident at Ban Padong.
Obviously, however, the co-operation of the parties is not the only condition which must be met to enable the commission to exercise full and effective control over the cease fire. The commission, in its report dated May 1, stated to the co-chairmen that it could set up effective machinery of supervision only if the co-chairmen were willing to supply adequate equipment including helicopters and light aircraft. On May 22 the commission provided the co-chairmen with a detailed list of technical requirements which again included an adequate number of helicopters and light aircraft. I remind the distinguished delegate from Poland that both these decisions were unanimous, and were concurred in by his commissioner in the field.
Now the Canadian commissioner in his reply to me sets out a list of the immediate requirements essential for the discharge of the commission, including three helicopters- later to be increased to six-and three light aircraft, together with the necessary maintenance and crews for both. In addition, he states a requirement of 20 jeeps and certain wireless sets.
His answer to the question of whether this kind of equipment can be obtained from the parties is that it would require double the amount of equipment and lead to endless difficulties in defining the territorial limits within which the aircraft and helicopters of each side could operate. This is a situation which would not end overnight even if there were a formal cease fire or political agreement reached among the various parties in Laos.
A further point raised by the Canadian commissioner in Laos is that reliance on Laotian parties for transport and other equipment would be wholly inconsistent with the commission's responsibility to this conference. The conference should deal promptly with this issue of whether the commission is to have the necessary equipment at its disposal and under its own independent control; and thereby free itself from the serious limitations of having to rely on others for its transportation needs.
90205-6-441
It must be clearly evident to all, Mr. Chairman, and really should not require a debate to establish that the ability of the commission to discharge its responsibilities in a fair and impartial manner cannot be made subject to the ability or willingness of one or other of the Laotian parties to provide transport and other necessary facilities. Just imagine the situation in which the commission would be placed if, before it could investigate any complaint against one of the parties, it not only would have to obtain the consent of that party to make the visit but also would have to rely on that party to furnish the transportation to the scene and then return the commissioners to the place from which they started. I find it very hard to believe it is the intention of the conference to reduce the commission which is its own agent to a position of impotence and indeed of exposure to ridicule.
This situation cannot and need not continue. Equipment in amounts adequate to the commission's immediate needs has been offered by the French and United States governments. All members have those offers in writing before them. The responsibility now lies fairly and squarely upon the two co-chairmen- the United Kingdom and the Soviet union -to see that this matter is settled. These offers cannot be ignored. The requirements of the commission cannot be ignored. They cannot be argued away. I suggest that without further ado the two co-chairmen should meet with representatives of the three members of the international commission to work out the practical details, consulting as necessary the governments that have made the offers of equipment and any other governments that might offer equipment. In this way, we can get the commission down to work on a practical basis, and we would go far to ensure the result and the success of this conference. I point out that the member nations of this conference cannot evade their responsibility to see that essential equipment is supplied to the commission.
