Delegation of the United States of America
June 16, 1961
Dear Mr. Co-Chairman:
I recall that on May 22 the international commission for supervision and control in Laos forwarded a list of its materiel requirements. This list was in response to the request by the co-chairman that the I.C.C. furnish them with information concerning its equipment needs. I also note that the commission in its letter to the parties in Laos of June 8, has expressed

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
its intentions of visiting and making investigations at various points in Laos. Therefore, it would seem that the commission has immediate need for at least some of the equipment it has requested.
The Minister of External Affairs of Canada, Mr. Green, specifically referred to the need for helicopters among other items in his statement to the conference of June 15. It is with this need in mind that I have been authorized by my government to offer to the co-chairmen and the commission three helicopters (Model H 34) for use by the I.C.C. in Laos. These can be provided within a few days after the acceptance of this offer.
I understand that the government of France has also offered equipment and support, and I hope that other governments represented at this conference will be able to do likewise. The United States government does not preclude the possibility of supplying other equipment or support should it be requested to do so.
The United States government expects that it will receive credit for any equipment it provides under this offer against its share of costs under such arrangements for financial support of the international commission for supervision and control as may be decided upon by the conference.

In its message of May 22, the I.C.S.C. in Laos expressed to the co-chairmen its unanimous recommendations as to the personnel and equipment which in its judgment would be required to carry out its functions. Since May 22 the Canadian delegation in Laos has not changed its views as to the requirements necessary for the proper functioning of the commission.
The Canadian delegation in Laos realizes, however, that it may take some time to engage the personnel and procure and dispatch the equipment which the commission has requested. In view of this fact it believes that it will be helpful to the co-chairmen to have an indication of the priorities which should be observed in fulfilling the commission's requirements so that what is immediately necessary may be dispatched without delay. The Canadian delegation in Laos therefore recommends most strongly that the following personnel and equipment be supplied to the commission at once as being essential for the discharge of its immediate responsibilities:
(a)	Three helicopters required immediately, and to be increased to six as soon as possible to ensure that four are always operational.
(b)	Three light aircraft with at least six-passenger capacity and capable of using short air strips and flying at ten thousand feet.
(c)	Maintenance organization for the helicopters and light aircraft to be established in Laos.
(d)	Pilots for the helicopters and light aircraft, preferably from India, Poland or Canada.
(e)	Twenty jeeps.
(f)	Wireless sets with two-hundred-mile range.
With the foregoing immediate needs in mind, the Canadian delegation in Laos has considered, in accordance with the co-chairmen's request, whether adequate transport and other requirements could be provided by the Laotian parties and has come to the following conclusions:
90205-6-441i
(a)	The provision of helicopters by the Laotian parties is not practical because neither side will agree to permit aircraft piloted by the opposition party to overfly territory occupied or disputed by them nor will the parties admit into the area forward or a defended locality helicopters piloted by the other side. Provision of helicopters by the parties would also mean twice the number held in readiness for commission use, since all investigations and visits by that means would involve double movement or double teams approaching trouble spots first from one side and then the other, whereas neutral helicopters should be able to move from one side to the other without delay or difficulty. The confused situation on the ground often makes clear demarcation of areas under the control of either side virtually impossible and thus the selection of a helicopter from either side for transportation will meet with objection for the reasons already stated. Consequently the commission would be prevented from supervising the cease fire in those disputed areas where available evidence indicates that violations are occurring unless it is equipped with its own helicopters and pilots and the objections of the parties to its movement in such areas are thereby overcome.
(b)	Provision of light aircraft by the parties is impracticable for reasons similar to those applying to helicopters.
(c)	Provision of vehicles has already proved beyond the capabilities of the parties. The commission representatives of Xieng Khou-ang are at present provided by Xieng Khou-ang parties with a total of three jeeps which are in such bad mechanical condition that the commission is having to consider purchase of replacement vehicles. Further, the commission is already supplying, at the request of the Xieng Khouang parties, petrol oil and lubricants for the vehicles allotted for its use there. The Vientiane party is also experiencing difficulty in meeting the minimum needs of the commission for transport in the Vientiane area, and for petrol, oil, and lubricants for vehicles allotted to the 'commission.
(d)	With regard to wireless sets, the responsibility for providing communications between teams and the commission headquarters has been undertaken by India. Communications are as important as transport to the ability of the commission to do its duty. It is essential that the equipment provided be standard and acceptable to the Indian communications officer, upon whom responsibility for the communications service rests.
(e)	The most important consideration of all is that reliance upon the Laotian parties for transport and other requirements would be wholly inconsistent with the commission's

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
responsibility for supervising the cease fire. Transport and communications are inseparable from commission operations. The commission must be independent of the parties in these respects if it is to retain its status as a neutral agency and be acceptable to all parties. The ability of the commission to discharge its responsibilities must not be subject to the ability or the willingness of one
or other of the Laotian parties to provide transport or other necessary facilities. Such a dependent position would place the commission under the control of the Laotian parties and nullify its capability for conducting impartial investigations. The interests of all the Laotian parties can be served only if the commission has the ability to move and administer itself independently.
